item.content:encoded:
7 de octubre de 2026 - 9:45 PM
Atlanta - Yoshinobu Yamamoto ponchó a 10 bateadores en siete entradas, Enrique “Kike” Hernández conectó un jonrón de dos carreras y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron 3-1 a los Braves de Atlanta el martes por la noche, tomando una ventaja de 2-1 en su Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Hernández, quien suele brillar en octubre, sacudió su decimoséptimo cuadrangular en postemporada, quebrando un empate con el miembro del Salón de la Fama de Béisbol Carlos Beltrán.
El boricua ahora está empate con Jim Thome, Aaron Judge y David Ortiz en la lista de jonrones en la postemporada.
Yamamoto dominó el muy esperado duelo contra el as de Atlanta, Chris Sale, quien permitió tres carreras y siete imparables en cinco entradas. Yamamoto, Jugador Más Valioso (MVP) de la Serie Mundial de 2025, concedió solo cuatro hits y una base por bolas, mejorando su récord de postemporada a 8-1.
Los Dodgers pueden ganar la serie —pactada al mejor de cinco juegos— y dar un paso más en su intento de convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional en ganar tres títulos consecutivos de Serie Mundial si vencen nuevamente a los Braves el miércoles por la noche en el cuarto partido.
Los Braves esperaban que dar descanso adicional a Sale fuera una fórmula ganadora para este crucial tercer encuentro. Sin embargo, tras dejar a seis corredores en base en las primeras tres entradas, permitió el jonrón de dos carreras de Hernández y un cuadrangular solitario de Freddie Freeman en el cuarto episodio.
Ozzie Albies abrió la novena entrada de Atlanta con un doblete contra el muro entre el jardín derecho y el central ante los lanzamientos de Edwin Díaz, avanzando a tercera base tras un rodado de out de Michael Harris II. Díaz dejó al corredor varado cuando Mauricio Dubón fue puesto out en un elevado de foul al jardín derecho y Mike Yastrzemski fue retirado con un rodado al campocorto Mookie Betts.
Tras una temporada agobiado por lesiones, Díaz se apuntó su primer salvado desde el pasado 14 de agosto, cuando lanzó la novena entrada en blanco contra Milwaukee.
FUe además su primer rescate de postemporada desde el 14 de octubre de 2024, cuanto se apuntó un salvamento por los Mets de Nueva York contra los propios Dodgers en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional.
Dubón realizó una atrapada saltando sobre la barda del jardín izquierdo para robarle un jonrón a Freeman en la tercera entrada; sin embargo, Freeman logró conectar su cuadrangular una entrada más tarde. El jonrón de Hernández hacia el jardín izquierdo impulsó a Andy Pages, quien había conectado un sencillo. Un out después, Freeman conectó el jonrón número 18 de su carrera en postemporada hacia el jardín derecho, ampliando la ventaja a 3-0.
El mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, bajó al bateador designado Shohei Ohtani al quinto puesto del orden al bate, debido a que Ohtani registraba un promedio de 3 de 15 en su carrera contra Sale. Ohtani se había ido de 4-0 con dos ponches ante Sale cuando los Dodgers perdieron 1-0 el 26 de agosto en Atlanta. Roberts predijo acertadamente que Ohtani tendría oportunidades con corredores en base al batear en una posición más baja del orden de bateo.
En la primera entrada, con corredores en primera y segunda, Sale ponchó a Ohtani para cerrar el episodio. En la tercera, con dos corredores en base, Ohtani llegó a primera gracias a una interferencia del receptor Drake Baldwin —lo que llenó las bases—, antes de que Miguel Rojas terminara la entrada con un elevado al jardín derecho. Ohtani recibió una base por bolas al abrir la octava entrada frente a Brent Suter, el cuarto lanzador de Atlanta.
Un rodado de Baldwin a primera base, con las bases llenas, impulsó a Dubón —quien había conectado un sencillo— en la quinta entrada, anotando así la única carrera de Atlanta ante Yamamoto.
Rojas abandonó el partido durante un turno al bate en la octava entrada. El segunda base pareció lastimarse la espalda al realizar un swing y fue sustituido por Tommy Edman. Los Dodgers informaron que la lesión consistía en dolor en la zona lumbar.
Tanner Scott sumó dos ponches en una octava entrada sin anotaciones para Los Ángeles.
Las noticias explicadas de forma sencilla y directa para entender lo más importante del día.

item.title: [WSLS] Yamamoto is dominant again as Dodgers ride homers from Hernández and Freeman to 3-1 win over Braves
item.dc:creator: Charles Odum; Associated Press
item.description: ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning. “I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator. Recommended Videos The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason. Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlan
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning.
“I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator.
Recommended Videos
The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason.
Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday night to take a 2-1 lead in their NL Division Series.
Yamamoto dominated his much-anticipated matchup with Atlanta ace Chris Sale, who allowed three runs and seven hits in five innings. Last year's World Series MVP permitted only four hits and one walk while improving to 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career postseason outings, including 10 starts.
His 10 strikeouts were a postseason high for him.
“I was confident and able to control all my pitches today,” Yamamoto said.
The Dodgers can clinch the best-of-five series and take another step toward becoming the first National League team to win three consecutive World Series by beating the Braves again Wednesday night in Game 4.
Atlanta hoped giving Sale extra rest would be a winning formula in the pivotal third game. Instead, after stranding six runners in the first three innings, he gave up the two-run homer to Hernández and a solo shot to former Braves star Freddie Freeman in the fourth.
“He was still touching 100 (mph),” manager Walt Weiss said of Sale. “The stuff was fine. Like I said, maybe the command not perfect. It wasn’t bad. But they did a nice job against him.”
That was all the offensive support Yamamoto and relievers Tanner Scott and Edwin Díaz would need.
Ozzie Albies opened the Atlanta ninth with a double off the right-center wall against Díaz and moved to third on Michael Harris II's groundout. Díaz stranded the runner and earned a save when Mauricio Dubón fouled out to right field and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to shortstop Mookie Betts.
A homer for the boo birds
Freeman said he didn't mind being booed by Atlanta fans in the sellout crowd of 42,420.
“I’ve got a gray uniform on,” Freeman said. “I expect boos. It’s OK. ... It’s all love. I still love everybody here and I’m looking forward to tomorrow.”
Dubón made a leaping catch over the left-field wall to rob Freeman of a home run in the third. Freeman wouldn't be denied an inning later. Hernández's homer to left drove in Andy Pages, who singled. One out later, Freeman pulled his 18th career postseason homer to right field for a 3-0 lead.
Lineup change
Roberts moved designated hitter Shohei Ohtani down to No. 5 in the lineup because Ohtani was 3 for 15 in his career against Sale. Ohtani went 0 for 4 with two strikeouts against Sale when the Dodgers lost 1-0 on Aug. 26 in Atlanta.
Roberts correctly predicted Ohtani would have opportunities with runners on base hitting lower in the order.
With runners on first and second in the first, Sale struck out Ohtani to end the inning. With two runners on base in the third, Ohtani reached on catcher's interference by Drake Baldwin to load the bases before Miguel Rojas ended the inning with a flyball to right field. Ohtani walked to lead off the eighth against Brent Suter, Atlanta's fourth pitcher.
Baldwin's bases-loaded grounder to first base drove in Dubón, who singled, in the fifth for Atlanta's only run.
Injury report
Rojas left during an at-bat in the eighth. The second baseman appeared to injure his back on a swing and was replaced by Tommy Edman. The Dodgers announced the injury as lower back pain.
Roberts said Rojas probably won't start on Wednesday and his availability off the bench will be determined before the game.
“I give him credit for conceding that at-bat,” Roberts said.
Weiss made a late change, moving Ronald Acuña Jr. from right field to designated hitter. Weiss said Acuña jammed his knee on a slide in Game 2. Acuña remained in the game but the knee was sore on Tuesday, leading to the lineup change.
Milestone win for Roberts
Roberts now has 71 career postseason wins, tying Tony La Russa for second-most in major league history. Joe Torre is first with 84.
Up next
Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle is expected to face Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow in Game 4 on Wednesday night. Mahle said Tuesday an abdominal pull is now a “non-issue.” He felt the pull before allowing one run in seven innings of a 4-3 loss to Philadelphia in 10 innings during the NL Wild Card Series last week.
___

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Dodgers beat Braves on Kiké Hernández and Freddie Freeman homers, take 2-1 NLDS lead
item.dc:creator: Maddie Lee
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article ATLANTA — The Dodgers went into Game 3 of the National League Division Series knowing they couldn’t be so reliant on the home run, especially with Braves ace Chris Sale on the mound. And yet, in a 3-1 win, it was the home run ball, paired with a masterful performance on the mound from right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, that secured the victory. The Dodgers pulled ahead to a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five series. The Dodgers tried to score in other ways, putting
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
ATLANTA — The Dodgers went into Game 3 of the National League Division Series knowing they couldn’t be so reliant on the home run, especially with Braves ace Chris Sale on the mound. And yet, in a 3-1 win, it was the home run ball, paired with a masterful performance on the mound from right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, that secured the victory.
The Dodgers pulled ahead to a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five series.
The Dodgers tried to score in other ways, putting on six baserunners in the first three innings of the game. But it didn’t work.
They failed to take advantage of some luck and poor defense from the Braves in the first inning, as Mookie Betts beat out a soft ground ball up the first base line and Teoscar Hernández reached on a fielding error by Braves shortstop Ha-Seong Kim.
Yoshinobu gives up four hits and strikes out 10 and Kiké Hernández hits a two-run home run to power the Dodgers to victory in Game 3 of the NLDS.
The lineup shuffling manager Dave Roberts did against Sale had superstar Shohei Ohtani, batting fifth, walking up to the plate with two outs and runners on first and second. His over-anxious approach at the plate so far this postseason followed him into the at-bat. And he struck out whiffing on a slider in the opposite batter’s box.
The next inning, Kyle Tucker hit a two-out single into left, baited Sale into picking over to first base twice, and then stole second. But he was stranded there, as Kiké Hernández went down swinging. All six of the Dodgers’ outs in the first two innings came via the strikeout.
In the third, the Dodgers loaded the bases. Mookie Betts started the effort with a double through the left side of the infield. And it looked for a moment as if Freddie Freeman had capitalized on the opportunity with a runner in scoring position.
He stayed back on a fastball and crushed it to deep left field, on a trajectory to just clear the short fence. But Braves left fielder Mauricio Dubón made a leaping catch, holding into the ball as he slammed into the wall.
Undeterred, the Dodgers kept putting runners on base. With two outs, Will Smith stayed through a slider to single. Ohtani clipped Braves catcher Drake Baldwin’s mitt and was awarded first base for catcher’s interference. Then Miguel Rojas, who’d exit the game in the eighth inning mid-at-bat with what the Dodgers called low back pain, hit a line drive that found leather to end the inning.
So, back to the long ball.
Perennial postseason hero Kiké Hernández delivered the first blow. With Andy Pages on first, after his first hit of the series, Hernández launched a changeup into the left-field stands. Then, two batters later, Freeman turned on an inside sinker and sent it over the right-field fence — where Dubón had no chance to track it down.
Game 3 was billed as a matchup between aces: Sale, whom the Braves tabbed for Tuesday because of his workload in their wild-card series, and Yamamoto, whom the Dodgers partially held back for the first two games with the NLCS in mind.
Yamamoto held up his end of the bargain, limiting the Braves to four hits and one run in seven innings.
He retired 10 of the first 11 batters he faced. The only baserunner in that time, Michael Harris II, bunted for a single. Yamamoto crashed hard, slipping on the slick grass as he tried to pivot but still managing to make a throw to first from the ground.
Shohei Ohtani is batting fifth in the lineup against Braves ace Chris Sale in Game 3 of the NLDS. He hasn’t hit fifth or lower in a starting lineup since 2020 with the Angels.
He only wavered in the fifth, loading the bases with a pair of singles and a four-pitch walk. The Braves’ batting order turned over, and Yamamoto got Baldwin to ground out to first, but that allowed a run. Then he induced Ronald Acuña Jr. to ground out to second to escape the jam. Rojas ranged to his left to field the ball and made an on-target throw even as he slipped on the grass in shallow right field.
Yamamoto didn’t allow another baserunner.
Left-handed reliever Tanner Scott served as the Dodgers’ setup man, throwing a hitless eighth. And right-hander Edwin Díaz came in for his first save opportunity since Aug. 14 against the Brewers.
He gave up a double off the wall to Ozzie Albies to open the inning but retired the next three batters.

item.title: [ABC7 Los Angeles] Dodgers land two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal in blockbuster deadline deal, sources say
item.dc:creator: Alden Gonzalez
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- For as much as they might have downplayed the possibility behind closed doors, the Los Angeles Dodgers were long seen by rival executives as overwhelming favorites to land generational ace Tarik Skubal. The Dodgers acquired Skubal, the reigning back-to-back American League Cy Young Award winner, from
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- For as much as they might have downplayed the possibility behind closed doors, the Los Angeles Dodgers were long seen by rival executives as overwhelming favorites to land generational ace Tarik Skubal. Their farm system was too good, their goals were too lofty, their rotation had become too uncertain.
On Saturday night, a day and a half before the trade deadline, they pulled it off.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal, the reigning back-to-back American League Cy Young Award winner, from the Detroit Tigers for a package of three prospects: outfielder Zhyir Hope, and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith, sources told ESPN's Jeff Passan.
Skubal, a 29-year-old pending free agent, will now headline what was arguably already the best rotation in the sport. Alongside him will be Yoshinobu Yamamoto, making a strong case for a Cy Young of his own, followed by Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani and Tyler Glasnow, all of whom are in varying stages of returning from injury.
The Dodgers had long touted their depth as a reason they didn't necessarily need Skubal. Snell, who has made one start all year, is expected to rejoin the rotation after his next rehab outing. Glasnow, out since May 6 with back spasms, will begin a minor league rehab assignment next week. And though Ohtani is still troubled by a sore left knee that only seems to bother him on the mound, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said earlier this week he fully expects him to pitch in October.
The Game 1 starter, though, will be Skubal, who might be the best pitcher in the world.
Skubal boasts a 2.79 ERA in 16 starts this year, striking out 116 batters and issuing 14 walks in 96 innings. The only thing that could stop him were bone chips that began to cause irritation in his left elbow in late April. Skubal underwent a less-invasive, revolutionary NanoScope procedure and returned in about six weeks. His ERA in July is 2.03. And as he addressed the media in the visiting clubhouse at Sutter Health Park in Sacramento late Saturday night, moments after being informed of the trade, Skubal at one point got choked up.
"Going into the season, this isn't what I planned on doing," Skubal said before getting on the verge of tears while reflecting on his time in Detroit. "But circumstances change, situations change. I'm very appreciative of everything that the Tigers have done for me."
A late bloomer who lasted until the ninth round of the 2018 draft, Skubal began to emerge as one of the game's most talented pitchers in 2022 and 2023 and took it to another level thereafter. From 2024 to 2025, Skubal went 31-10 with a 2.30 ERA and a whopping 469 strikeouts in 387 innings. His 12.6 FanGraphs wins above replacement led all major league pitchers.
When Skubal and members of the Tigers' front office exchanged arbitration figures in the ensuing offseason, the two sides were $13 million apart. An independent arbitrator ruled in favor of Skubal and his agent, Scott Boras, rewarding him a $32 million salary as he headed into his free-agent year.
Rumors had swirled throughout the offseason that the Tigers would trade him then. Instead, they doubled down, signing fellow starter Framber Valdez to a three-year, $115 million contract with the hope of winning the AL Central. Instead, the Tigers flopped. By the end of May, they were tied with the Colorado Rockies for the worst record in the majors, prompting executives throughout the industry to assume Skubal would be traded.
The Tigers proceeded to win 28 of their next 46 games, and suddenly it seemed as if Skubal might stay. But their momentum ran out. The Tigers lost back-to-back games to the last-place Kansas City Royals over the weekend and dropped two of three to the Baltimore Orioles thereafter. The last of those losses, on Wednesday night, saw Skubal take the mound and record his 1,000th career strikeout, then sit in the dugout while his team blew a 7-0 lead.
After it was over, the Tigers were seven games below .500, six games out of first place and three games out of a wild-card spot.
To many observing Skubal's availability, it was a death knell to his time in Detroit.
The Atlanta Braves, Chicago Cubs, Milwaukee Brewers, New York Yankees and Tampa Bay Rays were all in on Skubal to some extent, with the Brewers, deep in prospects, the favorites among that group. But the Dodgers were the clear frontrunners all along. And now they'll add Skubal to a laundry list of talent they've acquired from the outside over the years, following Ohtani, Snell, Yamamoto, Glasnow, Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and, this offseason, Edwin Diaz and Kyle Tucker.
The vast majority of those players came via free agency. The Dodgers loathe the high asking prices at midseason. But in getting Skubal, they parted from an outfield group that is stocked with talent -- one that is still headlined by Josue DePaula, a consensus top-25 prospect, along with Eduardo Quintero, ranked 45th on Kiley McDaniel's latest ESPN rankings. They also maintain all of their young major league starting pitching, namely Justin Wrobleski, Emmet Sheehan and Roki Sasaki.
In Hope and Ryan, though, the Tigers came away with two top-50 prospects.
Hope, 21, was slashing .293/.369/.530 with 23 home runs and 18 stolen bases for the Dodgers' Double-A affiliate and brings explosive power from the left side, top-tier speed and an ability to handle center field.
Ryan, 27, made a brief stint in the major leagues in 2024, putting up a 1.33 ERA in four starts. He then underwent a prolonged rehab from Tommy John surgery and has made eight starts in Triple-A, putting up a 4.46 ERA. He has been out since the middle of June with a hamstring injury, but McDaniel ranked him 49th in his midseason top 50 in May.
Smith, 21, was a third-round pick out of high school in 2023 who has put up a 3.88 ERA in 19 starts at the Class A level this season.
In three months, Skubal will head into the open market with the chance of signing the most lucrative deal ever rewarded to a starting pitcher. Before then, he will join a Dodgers club that boasts the highest run-differential and second-best record in the major leagues -- and help them try to become the first team in NL history to win three consecutive championships.
Asked his thoughts about joining the Dodgers, Skubal took about 15 seconds to compose himself before saying: "Yeah, it's exciting. I'm excited. They've got a good group."

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts Ponders Dodger Lineup Tweaks Ahead of Game 3
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta. The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2. With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly. Díaz Could Close “I think that we’ve buil
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta.
The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2.
With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly.
Díaz Could Close
“I think that we’ve built him up, regained the confidence in him and himself,” Roberts said of Díaz. “I think that it’s certainly a viable option for tomorrow night. I feel very confident with him finishing a game.”
Roberts said Díaz’s most recent outing was about as good as he has seen from him.
“That last outing was as good as we’ve seen him throw, and it’s hard to imagine throwing any better,” Roberts said. “He’s put himself in a position to be the closer.
“In October, I don’t pay too much attention to the long sample of a season in a lot of cases, because in October things happen quickly and you’ve got to be willing to read and react.”
Roberts also praised the way Díaz handled a difficult season.
“Character,” he said. “That’s the main thing. When things aren’t going the best and how players respond, that’s telling.
“The way he stayed the course, dealt with the injuries, went to OKC on a longer rehab to work things out and then took on whatever role we had for him says a lot about him.”
Lineup Changes Are on the Table
Roberts also acknowledged that the Dodgers could look different against Sale.
“I am considering it,” he said. “I think that’s a very fair question. I have to be mindful of it being two games, and then within those two games, what have I seen? Are we seeing good at-bats?”
He pointed to Will Smith as someone whose results have not matched the quality of his plate appearances.
“I think Will Smith is taking good at-bats, just missing some pitches, taking good swings, not chasing much,” Roberts said. “Versus other people maybe expanding, trying to do too much.
“Those are things that you’re trying to make bets on. Then you’re looking at tomorrow with Sale, the history, recency, how guys are prepared and will prepare for Sale. So yeah, I’m thinking through that, and there are possible changes.”
Roberts listed Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas and Max Muncy among the options he could work into the lineup.
“At the end of the day, our guys are our guys,” he said. “I can tweak a lineup. I can insert, take out a player or two, but we still have to go out there and play, execute and take good at-bats.”
Moving Ohtani Is Possible
Roberts said he would consider moving Ohtani further down in the order if he believes it helps the team.
“I would,” he said. “I think moving him from one to two, but going further than that, I’m open to it.
“If I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on. I know that undoubtedly.”
Roberts thinks some of Ohtani’s recent issues have come from trying to do too much.
“I think there’s a little bit of trying to do too much,” he said. “Everything orbits around Shohei in the sense of his talent, and the Braves are going to enter with caution. They’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them.
“Until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to use that playbook.”
He also said Ohtani may be pressing for power.
“Hitting homers, slugging is so much a part of his hallmark in the batter’s box,” Roberts said. “He’s very in tune with what’s being said, what he hasn’t done.
“But that base hit the other way yesterday, that’s production. Against a guy like Chris Sale, that gives you a chance. Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan given the starter.”
Roberts Still Believes in Pages
Andy Pages has also struggled, but Roberts said he plans to keep giving him chances.
“I’m going to continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re going to need him to be an active part of our team.
“This is, for me, given how he has come into the postseason, too small of a sample. He has taken two walks. Tomorrow is not going to be the end-all, be-all because Sale is a tough matchup, but I still want to see good at-bats.”
Roberts believes the main issue is pressing.
“I think there’s trying to do too much,” he said. “When he came back, he was swinging the bat really well, had success, and now I think there’s a little bit of trying too much.”
Freeman Looks Healthier
One hitter Roberts feels especially good about is Freddie Freeman.
“I think he’s gotten into his legs a lot more,” Roberts said. “He’s moving balls in the hitting zone forward. He’s as healthy as he’s been in quite some time. I think the mechanics are sound.”
Roberts credited the five-day break with helping Freeman get his knee into better shape.
“The week off was really crucial for him,” he said. “Being able to manage that with the five days off got him back to health to be able to work through some things without having to perform in a game setting.”
Sale vs. Yamamoto
Roberts expects Sale to attack the Dodgers much the same way he did when Atlanta faced them in August.
“The fastball just sort of bullied us at the top of the zone,” Roberts said. “There was some chase down below, and with the lefties, throwing more two-seamers to keep us honest in and then expand away.”
Still, Roberts believes the Dodgers are in a better offensive place than they were then.
“I do think we are in a different spot,” he said. “The stakes are certainly higher. There is familiarity on both sides. I think we’ll see better at-bats.
“Chris is going to be tough regardless. We know that. We know we’re going to be in for a dogfight, but I just don’t see him bullying us like he did his last start.”
And Roberts feels good about the pitcher the Dodgers will send out against him.
“There should be a lot of talk about Chris Sale, but our guy’s pretty dang good,” Roberts said. “He’s been a very good pitcher in the postseason, so we feel very good about that.
“I think both pitchers are going to pitch well. It’s kind of who grinds out at-bats best.”

item.title: [ABC7 Los Angeles] Dodgers lose 7th straight on D-backs' walk-off vs. Edwin Diaz
item.dc:creator: Follow ABC
item.description: PHOENIX -- The two-time defending World Series champions are in a rare funk. The Los Angeles Dodgers lost their season-high seventh game in a row in a stunning collapse Friday night after the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied for a 4-3 win when rookie Ryan Waldschmidt hit a two-run, walk-off homer against closer Edwin Diaz. "A loss is a loss, but to get walked off never feels good," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "We didn't play a clean game, a great game, on either side of the baseball, but we d
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- The two-time defending World Series champions are in a rare funk.
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost their season-high seventh game in a row in a stunning collapse Friday night after the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied for a 4-3 win when rookie Ryan Waldschmidt hit a two-run, walk-off homer against closer Edwin Diaz.
"A loss is a loss, but to get walked off never feels good," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "We didn't play a clean game, a great game, on either side of the baseball, but we did enough to put ourselves in position to win a game.
"Unfortunately, we couldn't finish it."
It was another rough outing for Diaz, who has an 11.00 ERA over 11 outings this season. The 32-year-old is a three-time All-Star, but he hasn't helped the Dodgers much after signing a three-year, $69 million deal during the offseason.
Waldschmidt connected on Diaz's hanging slider, hitting it into the left-center field seats for his second career homer and first big league walk-off.
"It's the slider," Diaz said. "The fastball was great today, but I missed the slider right in the middle. I think I was trying to be perfect with the pitch, and I'm missing right in the middle. I've got to be better. I'm a big league pitcher, so I've got to make pitches."
The Dodgers were swept by the Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs coming into Friday night's game. They still have a comfortable lead in the National League West -- 7 games in front of the Diamondbacks -- despite a 10-16 record since July 5.
Roberts acknowledged that Diaz has been struggling since his return from the injured list on July 29, but the manager wasn't necessarily ready to try a new closer. His reasoning was simple: There's no clear-cut alternative.
"Honestly, you've got to look at the options," Roberts said. "The way some of these guys are throwing, they're not throwing great either."
The Dodgers still look like a formidable team, particularly after adding ace left-hander Tarik Skubal in a trade-deadline deal with the Detroit Tigers last week. Two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell is slated to return Tuesday after missing most of the season because of injuries.
And the lineup still has plenty of star power with Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Kyle Tucker.
Roberts said before Friday's game that the remedy for the recent troubles was simple.
"We've just got to play better," Roberts said. "I don't think the standings -- I mean they're important, they matter -- but I just feel like with the talent we have, we've just got to play good baseball and it'll take care of itself. It always does."br/]

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Edwin Diaz Looking Like Postseason Bullpen X-Factor
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma

Diaz only needed 12 pitches to navigate his inning, striking out the first two batters on seven pitches before forcing a flyout from All-Star Drake Baldwin. In six innings since returning from the injured list in September, Diaz has only allowed one hit and walk while striking out 11 batters. The Dodgers didn’t win Sunday’s game in
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edwin Diaz came into Game 2 of the NLDS and continued his strong run of form, hurling a scoreless sixth inning with his team down a run.
Diaz only needed 12 pitches to navigate his inning, striking out the first two batters on seven pitches before forcing a flyout from All-Star Drake Baldwin. In six innings since returning from the injured list in September, Diaz has only allowed one hit and walk while striking out 11 batters.
The Dodgers didn’t win Sunday’s game in the end, but Diaz’s performance provided plenty of encouragement.
“Edwin was great,” manager Dave Roberts said. “If you look at tonight and try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining and certainly a positive.”
What Kept Edwin Diaz on the Injured List This Year?
Diaz looked to be as advertised for the Dodgers through the first couple of weeks of the season, but injuries impacted his production and made 2026 a season to forget. He held opponents to just one run through his first five appearances as a Dodger, but allowed three in consecutive appearances immediately afterwards before landing on the injured list with loose bodies in his elbow.
He came back from his elbow injury in July, but his struggles stuck with him over the following couple of weeks, as he allowed 11 runs across 7.2 innings pitched.
The right-hander landed back on the injured list Aug. 18 with neck inflammation, and remaind there for about a month. Since coming back, Diaz seems to have everything under control.
“It felt amazing,” Díaz said of his Game 2 outing. “That’s why I came here — to help this team win and pitch in big spots. … I want to keep getting the ball and doing my job.”
Will Edwin Diaz Take Over as the Dodgers’ Closer?
The Dodgers’ closer situation is uncertain at the moment, especially following Tanner Scott’s rough outing in Game 1 of the NLDS.
LA is clearly being cautious with Diaz’s situation given his results in the regular season, but if he continues to produce at a high level he could very well find himself in the mix to take over high-leverage situations in the late innings.
His next opportunity to make a difference for the Dodgers comes in Game 3 of the NLDS on Tuesday at 3:00 p.m. PT.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers Not Ruling Out Surprise Return From Injured Pitcher; Here's What It Could Mean
item.dc:creator: J P Hoornstra; Unknown
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts ruled pitcher Blake Treinen out for the postseason after the right-hander suffered a shoulder injury warming up for a relief appearance in San Francisco. Now, it sounds as if Roberts spoke prematurely. Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Saturday that Treinen's status for the postseason is "not decided firmly." "It was clear for this round," Friedman said, "but we'll keep monitoring it as we go." Friedman described the injury as
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts ruled pitcher Blake Treinen out for the postseason after the right-hander suffered a shoulder injury warming up for a relief appearance in San Francisco.
Now, it sounds as if Roberts spoke prematurely.
Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Saturday that Treinen's status for the postseason is "not decided firmly."
"It was clear for this round," Friedman said, "but we'll keep monitoring it as we go."
Friedman described the injury as "soreness" — a vague if much less ominous problem than the one Roberts suggested when Treinen was placed on the injured list after the Dodgers' Sept. 26 game against the Giants.
“I don't know if it was a complete blowout, but really unfortunate,” Roberts said at the time.
In 12 MLB seasons — the last six with the Dodgers — Treinen is 49-42 with a 2.94 ERA and 83 saves. Although he served as the Dodgers' closer only occasionally, he was a reliable source of strikeouts, low ERAs and some big postseason moments as the Dodgers captured three World Series championships this decade.
In 2024, Treinen saved three postseason games in three opportunities, allowing only three runs across nine October appearances. He was the winning pitcher in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series, when he threw 2.1 scoreless relief innings against the New York Yankees.
If the Dodgers need Treinen this month, it won't merely mean that he is healthy. It will mean somebody else — likely a couple somebodies — are not.
The Dodgers have enough quality and capable bullpen arms that they did not roster two pitchers who figured to be October mainstays (left-handers Justin Wrobleski and Jack Dreyer) in the National League Division Series. That decision was made in large part due to the Dodgers' opponent.
For Treinen to appear in a game this month, he'd have to prove more worthy of a roster spot than Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Brock Stewart, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Edgardo Henriquez, Edwin Diaz and Kris Bubic — plus Wrobleski and Dreyer.
Right-handers Bobby Miller and Emmet Sheehan have lockers and figure to be ready if called upon, too. Right-hander Will Klein finished the season on the injured list, like Treinen, but his throwing progression has put him in position to rejoin the roster if needed.
Treinen's possible availability is likely a mere footnote to the Dodgers' 2026 postseason run. Considering it sounded impossible a week ago, it's at least worth noting.

J.P. Hoornstra is an On SI Contributor. A veteran of 20 years of sports coverage for daily newspapers in California, J.P. covered MLB, the Los Angeles Dodgers, and the Los Angeles Angels (occasionally of Anaheim) from 2012-23 for the Southern California News Group. His first book, The 50 Greatest Dodgers Games of All-Time, published in 2015. In 2016, he won an Associated Press Sports Editors award for breaking news coverage. He once recorded a keyboard solo on the same album as two of the original Doors.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Edwin Díaz Looks Ready to Reassume Closer Role for Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Edwin Díaz gave the Dodgers one of their best moments in an otherwise frustrating Game 2 loss. The right-hander worked a clean sixth inning, struck out two and showed the kind of power stuff the Dodgers hoped to see when they added him. Díaz said afterward that the outing felt like a payoff for the work he has put in over the past couple of weeks. He also made it clear he is ready for whatever role Dave Roberts gives him. “I Was Throwing Strikes” “I think it was great,” Díaz sa
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Edwin Díaz gave the Dodgers one of their best moments in an otherwise frustrating Game 2 loss. The right-hander worked a clean sixth inning, struck out two and showed the kind of power stuff the Dodgers hoped to see when they added him.
Díaz said afterward that the outing felt like a payoff for the work he has put in over the past couple of weeks. He also made it clear he is ready for whatever role Dave Roberts gives him.
“I Was Throwing Strikes”
“I think it was great,” Díaz said. “I was throwing strikes. I was getting strike one against the hitters. I think the shape of the slider was great. The fastball movement was really good.
“I was just trying to do my job, keep the game close and give our team a chance to win.”
Díaz said the clean inning came after a lot of work on his mechanics.
“I’ve been putting a lot of work together the last maybe two weeks, week and a half, and today it played out,” he said. “I think today was really good.
“I just have to keep doing my job, keep helping this team win. When they give me the ball, I just want to keep the game on the line and see if we can win games.”
Ready for the Big Spots
Díaz has spent plenty of his career pitching in high-leverage spots, and he said getting that chance in October with the Dodgers was exactly what he wanted.
“It feels amazing,” he said. “That’s why I came here, to help this team win. I’m pitching in big spots, so I just want to keep getting the ball and doing my job.”
Asked whether he would be ready to pitch the ninth inning if Roberts called on him, Díaz kept it simple.
“I’m always ready,” he said. “I’ve been throwing the ball really good. In any situation they give me the ball, I’m just going to try to do my job.”
The Stuff Was There
Díaz touched 100 mph several times and said the postseason setting added a little extra energy.
“I feel really good,” he said. “My arm feels really good. My body feels great. It’s the playoffs, baby. Everything changes.
“Personally, I feel great. I was throwing strikes. I was letting the ball rip, and I was doing my job.”
He also believes his recent work has him trending back toward the form he showed last season.
“I think the last week I’ve been pitching really good,” Díaz said. “Last year I pitched great all season long. This season didn’t start the way everyone wanted, but I finished the regular season strong. I’m going to keep doing it right now (in the postseason).”

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts after Game 2 Loss: Dodgers Need to Sieze Chances
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Dave Roberts saw Game 2 as a reminder of how tough this series was always going to be. Atlanta pieced together a bullpen game, got key outs when the Dodgers had traffic on the bases and evened the NLDS before heading home. Roberts also made it clear that Blake Snell’s rough command was not tied to his recent groin issue. Snell simply fought his delivery, while the Dodgers kept missing chances to change the game. Snell Was Fighting His Delivery “He just was fighting himself with
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Dave Roberts saw Game 2 as a reminder of how tough this series was always going to be. Atlanta pieced together a bullpen game, got key outs when the Dodgers had traffic on the bases and evened the NLDS before heading home.
Roberts also made it clear that Blake Snell’s rough command was not tied to his recent groin issue. Snell simply fought his delivery, while the Dodgers kept missing chances to change the game.
Snell Was Fighting His Delivery
“He just was fighting himself with his delivery all game,” Roberts said. “I think the fastball was really good. The changeup was good at times, but in total he didn’t have fastball command, didn’t have slider command, and the changeup wasn’t there. He was pulling it.
“Overall, it wasn’t the groin. He just wasn’t sharp tonight.”
Roberts said there had been no warning signs before the game.
“Not at all. I thought that he wasn’t that sharp in San Francisco, but we got him out of it. Felt great coming out of that outing. He had an inning this past week, felt great, and then going into this start there were no concerns.
“You can tell when a pitcher, certainly with the lower half, isn’t right. Tonight the fastball was 97, 98, so it wasn’t compromised.”
Too Many Chances Left on the Bases
The Dodgers had runners on throughout the middle innings but could not come up with the hit that would have changed the game.
“That’s what it is,” Roberts said. “You look at Dubón in that first inning, puts the bat on the ball to drive in a run, infield hit. You look at Harris, 3-2, puts the ball in play in the gap, Olson running. We just had opportunities.
“We couldn’t get a hit when we needed to. We didn’t throw out a bunch of hits, but there was still traffic. We didn’t need many hits tonight to have a different result. We just couldn’t get it.”
Roberts felt good about the matchup when he found out Atlanta would use a bullpen game.
“Felt great. Felt great. Anytime I have Blake Snell lined up against any pitcher, I feel good. Getting Kerr out of the game and then getting Holmes out of the game, I felt really good where we were at. I really did.
“We just couldn’t execute as the game progressed.”
He also gave credit to Didier Fuentes for shutting the Dodgers down over 3 2/3 innings.
“I think it was just the fastball. Tonight you could see the fastball, it was 99, 100, and there were a lot of balls that we were just missing as far as lazy fly balls. We just couldn’t hit the ball flat against him.
“He was mixing in his split once in a while. At one point he retired nine straight guys. Two days off and doing what he did was pretty impressive.”
Roberts Wants Ohtani Back in the Zone
Shohei Ohtani has had a quiet start to the series, and Roberts said the biggest issue has been chasing pitches out of the strike zone.
“I think with Sho, if you look at the at-bats, there’s a lot of chase,” Roberts said. “It’s hard to square up and put good swings on balls that are out of the zone. That’s kind of what it boils down to.
“Certainly Sale is going to be tough because there’s a lot of strike to ball, high velocity, but it’s just trying to get him back in the hitting zone.”
Roberts said Ohtani has not reported any health issue.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine. This time of year everyone doesn’t feel perfect. He’s doing the best he can.
“He’ll be in there Game 3. We just have to take good at-bats and expect the best.”
Díaz Could Get a Ninth-Inning Look
One of the bright spots for Roberts was Edwin Díaz, who worked a clean inning and looked sharp.
“Edwin was great,” Roberts said. “If you look at tonight and try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining. That was certainly a positive.”
Asked whether Díaz could eventually get a chance to close, Roberts was direct.
“I’ve been very consistent in the fact that I wanted to get him an outing. This was a big spot, and he did what he needed to do. It looked great.
“Absolutely, you could see him closing. Yes, I can see him closing.”
A Three-Game Series Now
Roberts said Atlanta showed how aggressively it plans to use its pitching staff.
“They’re going to use any pitcher, try to get every matchup possible. Them pushing Fuentes to almost four innings, 40-something pitches, shows that they’re going to ride certain guys. Obviously, they use their bullpen accordingly.
“It’s a good team offensively. They’re going to fight. Harris is swinging a good bat. We knew it was going to be a battle. We knew those guys weren’t going to go down.
“We’re expecting Sale in Game 3, and we’ve got our work cut out. Now it’s a three-game series.”

Every subsequent trip to the plate, however, has been anything but. Granted, Ohtani has not been the Dodgers’ biggest problem offensively. Will
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers heroes, zeros from Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani still looks off
Heroes, zeros and the inside pitch from the Dodgers’ 3–2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in Game 2 of the National League Division Series:
Zero
Shohei Ohtani’s first at-bat of this NLDS looked relatively normal, as he pulled a 105 mph line drive into right for a first-inning, Game 1 single.
Every subsequent trip to the plate, however, has been anything but.
Granted, Ohtani has not been the Dodgers’ biggest problem offensively. Will Smith (0–for–8), Andy Pages (0–for–7, one walk) and Tommy Edman (0–for–5, one walk) are all vying for that honor.
But if there was any hope that the team’s playoff-opening bye week would fix the two-way amid his ongoing right arm and left knee injuries, these two games have been a reminder of just how far he is from his typical self.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine,” manager Dave Roberts said.
But…
“I don’t know if he’s trying to do too much because he doesn’t feel perfect,” the skipper added, in what felt more like a tacit acknowledgement.
A healthy Ohtani, after all, wouldn’t go 0–for–2 against plucky feel-good story Ray Kerr, striking out on an inside fastball in the first inning before popping out in a key spot with two aboard in the third.
A healthy Ohtani wouldn’t need to slap the ball the other way Ichiro-style just to get a base hit, as he did on his lone single in the fifth.
The most telling thing for the 32-year-old superstar the last two days?
The Braves haven’t been afraid to challenge him, throwing him nine fastballs in the middle-third of the strike zone so far. And he hasn’t been able to punish them for it, turning only one into a hit (that first-inning, Game 1 single) while also chasing more outside of the zone after failing to end his at-bats.
“He’ll be in there Game 3,” Roberts confirmed. “We’ve just got to, again, take good at-bats and expect the best.”
Hero
At least the Dodgers’ other pre-NLDS injury question mark has seemingly turned a corner.
In his final 66 games of the regular season (going back to July 5), Freddie Freeman had hit only one home run. In September, he slumped to a .184 average with only one extra-base hit while battling a right knee injury that threatened to linger into the playoffs.
However, the bye week seemingly did wonders for him, following up a one-hit, one-walk performance in Game 1 of the series with a two-hit night Sunday that included a solo homer to right field.
“I feel good, so I think we can be done with those questions,” he quipped when asked about his swing and knee injury. “Just more consistently getting myself in a good spot, being able to put good swings on it.”
Unsung hero
There were times this year when Edwin Díaz’s fastball velocity dipped as low as 92 mph.
During his scoreless appearance in the sixth inning on Sunday, the resurgent right-hander dialed it up to a season-high 100.8 mph.
That was just one impressive aspect of Díaz’s latest standout performance, in which he extended his scoreless streak to six innings (including 15 straight batters retired over his last five outings) since returning from his second injured list stint of the year on Sept. 18.
“Edwin was great,” Roberts said. “I think if you look at tonight, try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining and certainly a positive.”
Key stat
Zero: As in 0 hits with runners in scoring position for the Dodgers on Sunday, and 0 runs scored via any method other than a home run so far in this NLDS.
Ironically, the club’s lack of power had been the bigger concern coming into the playoffs.
While they could be (extremely) up-and-down in the regular season in situational at-bats, they still rank seventh in batting average with runners in scoring position and third in OPS.
That, however, hasn’t translated to October yet.
“Got to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” Freeman said. “I think that’s our biggest thing right now.”
Quote of the night
“We’ve been in tougher spots than this one,” outfielder Teoscar Hernández said, when asked how crucial the team’s past October experience (especially in back-and-forth series like the 2024 NLDS and 2025 World Series) would be in the face of what is now a best-of-three showdown. “It’s a 1–1 series. We know they’re going to have the best pitcher that they have, starting pitcher, in [Game 3 with Chris] Sale. But we’re just gonna try to be ready and just go with the best plan and just try to execute it.”

item.title: [ABC7 Los Angeles] Dodgers' Evan Phillips back 13 months after Tommy John surgery
item.dc:creator: Follow ABC
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- Reliever Evan Phillips was reinstated off the injured list Monday, returning to the Los Angeles Dodgers 13 months after having Tommy John surgery. The 31-year-old right-hander spent the last month at Triple-A Oklahoma City, where he had a 1.80 ERA with 13 strikeouts and five walks in 10 innings over 12 games for the Comets. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Reliever Evan Phillips was reinstated off the injured list Monday, returning to the Los Angeles Dodgers 13 months after having Tommy John surgery.
The 31-year-old right-hander spent the last month at Triple-A Oklahoma City, where he had a 1.80 ERA with 13 strikeouts and five walks in 10 innings over 12 games for the Comets.
"My primary mix is very sharp and ready to roll," he said before the Dodgers defeated the Colorado Rockies8-7 in 11 innings.
Phillips, who did not appear in Monday's win, had the surgery in May 2025, setting him on course for the first long-term rehab stint of his career.
"Credit to myself to stick with the process, leaning a lot on my family and my teammates here," he said. "I was very appreciative to spend my rehab here last year after the injury. I think that helped my mindset stay focused as well. Just ready for this next step."
Phillips won't be needed again in the closer role. Tanner Scott has been ably filling in for injured Edwin Díaz, who went on the IL in April for loose bodies in his elbow.
Phillips figures to slot into a middle-relief position as he builds up to a potentially bigger role in October, when the NL West-leading Dodgers are expected to seek a third consecutive World Series championship.
During his month in the minors, Phillips spent his first several games focused on the physical side of pitching, including experimenting with grips, location, and working on a changeup. Then he flipped the switch.
"The second half of it I really tried to step up the execution and competition side of things," he said. "That way, hopefully, it's not the first time I'm doing it here."
In a corresponding move, the Dodgers optioned right-hander Paul Gervase to Triple-A a day after he tossed two scoreless innings with two strikeouts against San Diego. Left-hander Jake Eder was released.
In other moves, the team added pitcher Carlos Duran to the 40-man roster and designated catcher Chuckie Robinson for assignment.
Duran, a 24-year-old right-hander, appeared in 30 games for Triple-A Oklahoma City, going 2-2 with a 3.86 ERA this season. He had 50 strikeouts in 35 innings while limiting hitters to a .203 average. He made his major league debut last season with the Athletics.

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Dodgers Could Use Four Different Closers This Postseason
item.dc:creator: Jordon Lawrenz
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are eyeing a historic three-peat, and it's going to take an incredible pitching staff to do so. This team's offense is what it is, but there are still questions regarding the bullpen, specifically at the end of games. Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, and Edwin Diaz were all named by one of t
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are eyeing a historic three-peat, and it's going to take an incredible pitching staff to do so.
This team's offense is what it is, but there are still questions regarding the bullpen, specifically at the end of games.
Manager Dave Roberts recently had a chance to speak with the media, and according to Dodgers Nation, he's confident in four different players to close out games this October.
Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, and Edwin Diaz were all named by one of the best skippers the league has ever seen, but ultimately it will come down to what Roberts is feeling in each given situation, along with how each reliever has performed up to that point.
Dodgers can afford to be flexible
At this point in the year, all bets are off. Starting pitchers come in as relievers, closers are asked to open games, simply put, everything is on the table.
Going into the National League Division Series, Roberts said it's "easy to see" Scott finishing games.
He then added that will vary by game, and if an opportunity presents itself to use Scott in the eighth inning, that's exactly what this team will do.
The Dodgers are the back-to-back World Series Champions for a reason, and it's partly due to the brilliant mind that Roberts has.
He said he feels "very comfortable" with Sasaki, Phillips, and Diaz closing out games.
Diaz's struggles have been well-documented, though injuries may have played a huge part in all of that.
Phillips has just one save this season, but that doesn't mean the 32-year-old isn't built for the bright lights.
Finally, Sasaki will remain a mainstay of this team's bullpen in a similar role to what he did a year ago with his three postseason saves and two holds in nine appearances.
Is Scott the obvious choice?
On paper, if everything goes according to plan, there's no reason for the Dodgers not to use Scott in the ninth inning.
This is a guy who was tied for 14th in the league with his 25 saves, and he has a WHIP under 1.00 (0.99) which is incredibly impressive.
Regardless, Scott has picked up a save in his last three appearances. He's coming into the NLDS well-rested, and that's even with him earning a pair of saves at the end of the Dodgers regular season.
Keep in mind, Scott's last four appearances were all against the sub-par San Francisco Giants, and he did blow a pair of saves in the month of September.

item.title: [dodgersway.com] Dodgers shouldn’t give Blake Treinen the Evan Phillips treatment after season-ending injury

item.content:encoded:
Whenever the Los Angeles Dodgers playoff journey ends, they'll need to make several decisions on how to fortifiy the bullpen. Much like playoff time last season, the unit has become a house of cards that feels as if it's on the verge of collapse, even if there's been good news recently.
One player who won't be part of the postseason bullpen is veteran right-hander Blake Treinen. He suffered a shoulder injury while warming up in the bullpen during September 26's matchup against the San Francisco Giants. The full extent isn't yet known, but it is significant enough for the Dodgers to announce that the 38-year-old is done for the year.
Treinen is a free-agent-to-be, and that sets the scene for Los Angeles to make a decision. Does the club let the long-time high-leverage hurler walk? Or does the team follow the route it took with Evan Phillips, whom they re-signed while he was recovering from Tommy John surgery, with hopes that he could return as an impact bullpen arm down the stretch?
It's time for the Dodgers to thank Blake Treinen for his service and let him ride off into the sunset
Listening to some of his peers talk about the injury, it's clear that Treinen is a well-liked and influential player within the Dodgers' bullpen.
“It’s gut-wrenching for us,” Alex Vesia said, via Jack Harris of the California Post. “Blake’s one of our leaders out there in the bullpen.”
We're not going to say that veteran leadership doesn't matter, but there are a few key differences between Treinen's situation and the circumstances surrounding Phillips at the time that LA decided to bring him back.
The first has to do with age. Phillips is six years younger, and that matters. If Treinen were to come back and try to pitch in 2027, it would be for his age-39 season, making it extremely questionable as to whether or not he'd have anything left in the tank.
Timing matters too. As we saw with Phillips this year, it can take a bit for an injured reliever to get back into the groove. The 32-year-old was horrendous when he came back in July, throwing 7⅓ innings and surrendering five earned runs, including four home runs, before settling in to post a 2.41 over his final 18⅔ innings from August 1 onward. Even then, he didn't fully hit his stride until September.
The injuries these two relievers have suffered are different, but the thought remains the same. Treinen was also up and down this year, posting a decent 3.64 ERA, which means he might not have that extra gear that Phillips does.
The most important difference, however, is that Phillips had been mostly healthy before his UCL injury, whereas Treinen has dealt with a variety of maladies in recent years. He was limited to just 29⅔ innings this season and missed nearly two months with elbow inflammation. He dealt with forearm soreness in 2025 that limited him to just 26⅔ innings, dealt with a hip issue in 2024, and missed the entire 2023 campaign after undergoing shoulder surgery to repair his labrum and rotator cuff.
In fact, Treinen hasn't had a fully healthy year since 2021, so while he's put together dominant campaigns in the past, it's hard to expect him to be that same pitcher and avoid other injuries moving forward.
This should also be a lesson for the Dodgers, who have spent big on veteran relievers only to get mediocre results and a bunch of injuries. Relievers are volatile, and we saw that from Tanner Scott last year. We saw how quickly they can run out of gas with the Kirby Yates experiment. We're in the throes of it right now with Edwin Diaz.
The lesson from Phillips should be clear. Los Angeles originally acquired him off waivers from the Tampa Bay Rays in 2021. The Dodgers got him as a young player and made him into what he is today through their coaching and development plan. They need more of that and less star chasing in the pen, because the latter is more often than not a disappointment.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dodgers Well Represented on Year-End NL Leaderboards
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — With the end of the regular season on Sunday, the statisticians can finally put down their pencils. We had a near miss for the triple crown in the American League (Yordan Alvarez) and a pitcher with a sub-2.00 ERA in the National League (Jacob Misiorowski). item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — With the end of the regular season on Sunday, the statisticians can finally put down their pencils. We had a near miss for the triple crown in the American League (Yordan Alvarez) and a pitcher with a sub-2.00 ERA in the National League (Jacob Misiorowski). And though no Dodgers were at the top of any statistically categories this year, there were plenty featured in the NL Top Ten. Let’s do a quick end-of-season rundown, shall we?
The plan for two-way dominance Cy Young/MVP consideration sort of flamed out before the All-Star break, and Shohei was struggling to find his footing at the plate in the aftermath of a couple of injuries (most notably his right knee). However, even a diminished Ohtani is among the league’s elite and Shohei did enough in the first half of the season to lock down some Top-Ten finishes. He was tied for ninth in home runs with 30, tied for tenth in walks with 81, and 19th in batting average with .275. His other numbers were also top-ten-worthy: he finished sixth in the NL in On-Base Percentage with .377 and fifth in slugging percentage with .512. And, finally, his OPS of .889 was more than 100 lower than last year, but still third in the league behind Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong and the Nationals’ James Wood.
It was good year. But considering the wow factor of the first two years, a bit of a disappointment. Hopefully, he can get right in time to do damage like the old Shohei in the playoffs.
Despite his mighty struggles in September, Freddie turned in another strong campaign in 2026. Although his power number were down considerably, he still found his way on base at a clip not often seen in the modern game. Though his .288 batting average represented a low in Freddie’s Dodger years, it was still good enough for tenth place in the league. And, his 167 hits put him in eighth place in that category.
For those of you keeping track, he now stands at 2,598 hits in his career, 402 shy of the 3,000 mark that he’s had on his mind for a while. He’ll probably need three more years in the big league to reach that plateau, so that means the Dodgers would have to re-sign him after his current contract expires at the end of next year. Will that happen? It should, but I don’t know if Andrew Friedman wants to be sentimental about such things.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto was the only Dodger pitcher who logged enough innings to qualify for postseason awards, and he’s sure to get at least a sniff or two in the Cy Young voting. His year was probably his best yet: Fifth in wins (14), 3rd in ERA (2.53), 4th in innings pitched (185), 10th in strikeouts (182), 2nd in WHIP, and 2nd in Average Against (.182). Of course, all the hardwares going to the Miz this year, but Yamamoto’s steadiness is something to behold even if he doesn’t light up the radar gun on every pitch.
After a horrible year in 2025, no one was quite sure what to expect from Tanner Scott in 2026, and when Edwin Diaz went out with injury, there were more than a few Dodger fans who dreaded the thought of last year’s goat closing out games. However, Scott proved more than up to the task, converting 25 of 29 save opportunities, which put him in sixth place in the NL leader board. It will be interesting to see what happens as a resurgent Edwin Diaz seems to be ready for a return to the closer’s role.
Honorable mention….
Though they didn’t make any top tens, we should give it for Max Muncy, who made the All-Star team and finished 13th in the league in OPS and tied for 14th in the NL for homers. A really solid season from Max. Alex Vesia finished 7th in the league in appearances, and had an impact on more games than you might think. And, though they’re nowhere on the leaderboard, the strong finishes for Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez, and Kyle Tucker gives one hope for the postseason.
What about the team?
Since the Dodgers won the second most games in baseball, it only figures that they’d have a lot of nice numbers at the end of the year. On the hitting side, they finished fourth in home runs (204), fourth in RBI (756), 3rd in batting average (.257), second in slugging percentage (.424), and second in OPS (.762).
On the pitching side, they finished second in team ERA (3.55), 3rd in strikeouts (1,521), first in WHIP (1.18), and first in average against (.218). When you isolate the starters, the numbers are even better: first place in ERA, WHIP, and average against, and second in strikeouts.
The bullpen was good, but closer to the middle of the pack in the NL: fourth in ERA, fourth in saves, and fourth in WHIP. One stat that may work in the pen’s favor though: they finished 14th out of 15 NL teams in bullpen innings pitched. That means that other pens (save the Phillies) have been taxed more than the Dodgers. That could make a difference the deeper we go into October.
Conclusion
The numbers show kind of how 2026 felt: it was a good year, but not a dominant year. Many players, while still contributing, were down from their historical norms. And if the past is prologue, look for a lot of low-scoring games this October. Games that might be decided by one swing of the bat or one shut-down inning.
In the meantime, we wait. We watch and we wait.
See you Saturday!
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
Now that the 2026 MLB regular season is done, Sony made one last ratings tweak for many of the players across the league on October 2. The October MLB The Show 26 ratings update saw Mookie Betts & Cade Smith rise to join the other Diamonds in the game.
The notable changes
Mookie Betts is back as a Diamond in MLB The Show 26. He and Cade Smith were the only two to move to Diamond status on October 2. Betts moved to 85 OVR after a strong final few weeks. Over his last 14 games, Betts slashed .316/.418/.632 with four home runs and 10 extra-base hits.
Smith, meanwhile, notched 41 saves and struck out 107 batters over 74 innings this season for the Guardians.
Fernando Tatis Jr. moved up three points between the last update and now. Tatis Jr., before the start of the playoffs, hit five home runs and nine extra-base hits in the last 15 games of the regular season for San Diego.
Elly De La Cruz, who had eight extra-base hits in the final two weeks, moved to 87 OVR, a +2 OVR increase. He moved there, along with NL Wild Card hero Michael Harris II.
As for who went down, Yandy Diaz and Jacob deGrom were both downgraded from Diamond status.

item.title: [yardbarker.com] Dodgers NLDS Notes: Edwin Díaz, Edgardo Henriquez & Starting Rotation
item.dc:creator: Matthew Moreno
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers earned the benefit of a postseason bye and now are reaping the full benefit as the Philadelphia Phillies staved off elimination to force the Atlanta Braves to a winner-take-all Game 3 in their Wild Card Series matchup. The winner advances to face the Dodgers in the National League Division Series, which begins Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The start for time for Game 1 has not yet been decided as it hinges on whether or not the San Diego Padres or Chicago Cubs reach the NLD
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers earned the benefit of a postseason bye and now are reaping the full benefit as the Philadelphia Phillies staved off elimination to force the Atlanta Braves to a winner-take-all Game 3 in their Wild Card Series matchup.
The winner advances to face the Dodgers in the National League Division Series, which begins Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The start for time for Game 1 has not yet been decided as it hinges on whether or not the San Diego Padres or Chicago Cubs reach the NLDS to play the Milwaukee Brewers.
In the meantime, the Dodgers are spending the rest of the week going through workouts and simulated games, much like their approach in 2024 that proved beneficial.
The Dodgers avoiding the Wild Card Series this year has proven beneficial for multiple players dealing with an injury, including Edgardo Henriquez.
He missed the final two weeks because of lower back discomfort but has made steady progress in his recovery and is on track for the NLDS.
“We’ll get him some work this week. He’s trending really well at this point,” Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes said on Tuesday. “His last live BP went well, he’s responding positively after he throws and isn’t feeling any lingering discomfort.
“We’ve still got a few steps to go, but if that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster.”
Elsewhere in the Dodgers bullpen, Edwin Díaz finished the regular season on a high note after returning from a stint on the 15-day injured list because of a neck issue.
“I don’t know if we could have asked much more out of Edwin. I think it was, like, a 50-plus percent strikeout rate when he came back,” Gomes noted. “Felt like each outing was more and more sharp, and looking more like himself.
“Feels like he’s in a great place right now, stuff out of hand is as good as it’s been all year, and we know that he has pitched in the hottest of hot games in the past, and in any role, especially in the postseason. He’s looked great and glad that he’s in the position that he’s in and was able to bounce back after the IL stint.”
Díaz threw five scoreless innings, allowed just one hit and one walk while collecting nine strikeouts across five appearances upon getting activated Sept. 18. While Gomes projected confidence, what may still be different for Díaz is he’s not relied upon as the primary closer.
Even without Shohei Ohtani pitching, the Dodgers are heading into the playoffs with a formidable starting rotation that consists of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. What order they will pitch in has not yet been decided.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said the team would not set their NLDS rotation until Thursday, at which point they would know whether the Braves or Phillies advanced.
“I say that because just trying to figure out opponent and the schedule going forward, not sure about game times and things like that. We’re having conversations but we’re not definitive yet,” Roberts explained.
“I think opponent certainly should matter, could matter. Talking to Mark Prior about where guys are at. To be honest, we could really put all four guys in a hat and run them out there. But I think there is going to be more thought behind it. We don’t need to make a decision right now, so really just trying to be clear and talk through it.”
Last year the Dodgers almost exclusively used Snell (Wild Card, NL Championship Series and World Series) as their Game 1 starter. Ohtani started against the Phillies in the opener of the NLDS.
One change from the 2025 postseason is Glasnow’s first appearance likely won’t come out of the bullpen during the NLDS due in part to a different schedule.
