item.title: [Dodgers Way] Dodgers get Edgardo Henriquez update as postseason bullpen picture comes together
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: One of many things that makes the Los Angeles Dodgers so infuriating to competitors is how lucky they get when it comes to injuries. Over their last three seasons, their pitching staff has been riddled with shoulder inflammation and elbow impingements, and so on — but they always seem to get their key players back exactly when they need them. They might have lost Blake Treinen in their last series of this season, but he's had a tough year and wasn't a lock for the postseason roster anyway. The r
item.content:encoded:
One of many things that makes the Los Angeles Dodgers so infuriating to competitors is how lucky they get when it comes to injuries. Over their last three seasons, their pitching staff has been riddled with shoulder inflammation and elbow impingements, and so on — but they always seem to get their key players back exactly when they need them.
They might have lost Blake Treinen in their last series of this season, but he's had a tough year and wasn't a lock for the postseason roster anyway. The real concern was for Edgardo Henriquez, who's been missing since September 14 with lower back discomfort.
Henriquez was officially activated from the IL on Tuesday, but his status ahead of the NLDS still seemed touch-and-go, given how fresh off injury he'll be with zero runway.
There are still boxes he has to check, but Dodgers GM Brandon Gomes said on Tuesday that he's trending the right direction. Katie Woo reported, "should he come out of all bye-week activities (live hitters, sim games, etc), he'll be on the NLDS roster."
The back end of the Dodgers' bullpen has no clear hierarchy right now, so Henriquez would be a welcome addition for later innings.
Edgardo Henriquez trending positively toward returning for Dodgers' NLDS
It's hard to guess what Dave Roberts' trust tree might look like heading into October. Tanner Scott, Edwin Díaz, and Tanner Scott are the obvious closing options, but Scott posted a 4.15 ERA in September, Díaz showed signs of life after his IL stint but still isn't truly trustworthy, and there's no telling if Sasaki will turn back into the lights-out closer he became last season.
The Dodgers used Henriquez as early as the third and as a late as extra innings over the course of the regular season, but he picked up two saves in nine games finished this year. His ability to throw 100+ MPH with regularity is his greatest asset, as long as he can control his pitches.
He was trending toward a more regular eighth- or ninth-inning role before he got hurt, as the Dodgers had to go with closers by committee with Díaz's absences and Scott struggling a little more. Henriquez has been effective anywhere between the seventh and ninth, with just a .191 batting average and .553 OPS against.
The Dodgers' bullpen being as shaky as it still is, the onus will be on the starters (again) to go as deep into games as possible, but Henriquez's presence should add a little more assurance.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula, bench shuffle
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA. One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered. Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers to get ‘huge impact’ with key reliever on track for NLDS return
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: Over the last two months of the regular season, no team had a more productive bullpen than the Dodgers. And come the start of their postseason trek on Saturday, the team might be adding another key arm back to the group. General manager Brandon Gomes announced on Tuesday that the club expects to have hard-throwing right-handed reliever Edgardo Henriquez available for its National League Division Series, an encouraging development after Henriquez missed the final couple weeks of the regular seaso
item.content:encoded:
Over the last two months of the regular season, no team had a more productive bullpen than the Dodgers.
And come the start of their postseason trek on Saturday, the team might be adding another key arm back to the group.
General manager Brandon Gomes announced on Tuesday that the club expects to have hard-throwing right-handed reliever Edgardo Henriquez available for its National League Division Series, an encouraging development after Henriquez missed the final couple weeks of the regular season with a strain in his back.
Prior to getting hurt, Henriquez was emerging as one of the top arms in the Dodgers’ resurgent relief corps (which led all MLB bullpens in August and September with 4.3 combined wins above replacement, according to Fangraphs, and ranked fourth in that stretch in combined ERA at 3.20).
A 24-year-old former prospect who has started to routinely eclipse 103 mph with his fastball, Henriquez ranked fourth among the team’s relievers (minimum 20 appearances) with a 2.85 ERA this season. He also struck out 70 batters in 60 total innings and converted each of the ninth-inning save opportunities he received.
Henriquez had hit his stride in August and early September, allowing just one run in a 17-game stretch that featured 25 strikeouts and only two walks and seven hits allowed.
However, after giving up two runs in a Sept. 13 appearance in Miami against the Marlins, he went on the IL with his back injury –– one that initially cast doubt on his postseason availability.
Luckily for the Dodgers, Henriquez’s status has improved since then. He resumed a throwing during the team’s final regular-season homestand. He recently completed a session of live batting practice without feeling any lingering discomfort. And while Gomes said “we still got a few steps to go” before Henriquez gets the green light to return, every indication is that he should be available for the club’s best-of-five NLDS.
“If that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster,” Gomes said.
“Given the body of work, what he’s done, the unique skill set, that could be huge for us,” manager Dave Roberts added, before correcting himself: “Will be huge for us.”
Indeed, Henriquez would figure to occupy a high-leverage spot in the Dodgers’ postseason bullpen. He gives them not only a trustworthy right-hander option –– along with Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart and the recently resurgent Edwin Díaz –– but also one of the biggest fastballs in the game.
Henriquez’s 100.7 mph average fastball velocity ranked second among MLB pitchers this season, behind only star Padres closer Mason Miller. The team’s next-hardest thrower is Sasaki, whose heater averaged only 97.9 mph this year (though could increase in the playoffs as he shifts to a bullpen role).
Last October, Henriquez was a mixed bag in the playoffs. In two of his appearances (Game 1 of the wild card series and Game 5 of the World Series), he failed to record an out while allowing a hit and two walks in both outings. But in the other (Game 3 of the World Series), he pitched two scoreless frames in the team’s marathon 18-inning win, becoming an unsung hero in their Fall Classic triumph.
This time, Henriquez is set for a prominent role, assuming he gets through one more session of live batting practice OK.
“[He would make a] huge impact,” Roberts said. “I think he’s one of those guys that getting the bye has really benefited.”

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Dodgers Expect Edgardo Henriquez Back for NLDS If Final Tests Go Well
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez is “trending really well,” according to general manager Brandon Gomes, and he is looking likely to be on the NLDS roster. Henriquez is still on the injured list with a lower back injury, which shut him down for the last two weeks of the regular season. Edgardo Henriquez injury status When speaking to the media, including Dodgers Nation, on Tuesday, September 29th, Gomes said Henriquez threw a live batting practice session against hitters, and it wen
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez is “trending really well,” according to general manager Brandon Gomes, and he is looking likely to be on the NLDS roster.
Henriquez is still on the injured list with a lower back injury, which shut him down for the last two weeks of the regular season.
Edgardo Henriquez injury status
When speaking to the media, including Dodgers Nation, on Tuesday, September 29th, Gomes said Henriquez threw a live batting practice session against hitters, and it went well.
Henriquez also has additional activities lined up during the bye week to clear up, including simulated games and more live batting sessions.
If he clears the remaining checkmarks, Henriquez will be ready for the NLDS, per Gomes.
“We’ve still got a few steps to go, but if all that goes well, the expectation is he will be on the roster,” the general manager said.
What will Henriquez’s role be with the bullpen?
Before he got hurt, Henriquez was a set-up man for the Dodgers, and he was also a budding closer for the team thanks to his consistency.
Tanner Scott is prone to home runs, while Edwin Diaz was in a spiral, which helped Henriquez emerge as the most consistent relief pitcher.
Over the last few weeks, Scott has been steady, while Diaz has rebuilt himself from the ground up. Additionally, Roki Sasaki moved into the bullpen, leading the Dodgers into the postseason with plenty of candidates to close, Henriquez among them.
“Obviously we’ve had a lot of talent over the years,” manager Dave Roberts said. “But as far as sitting here today at the end of the season, it’s as good of shape as we’ve ever been in with the bullpen.
“That could change in a day, in a game, as we all know. But right now, feel really good about everyone out there.”
Roberts is known for making bullpen decisions based on feel in the postseason, and depending on how Henriquez looks coming back, he may close or perhaps settle into a middle relief role.
Luckily, the Dodgers have bullpen options, which hasn’t been the case for a while.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Dodgers' Josue De Paula update all but confirms his postseason roster spot
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers completed their sweep over the San Francisco Giants on Sunday in extra innings. It was their sixth time reaching the century-mark during the last decade, which is better than any American League team and second only to the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League. The Dodgers now have four days to game plan before they take on either the Philadelphia Phillies or the Atlanta Braves in the NLDS at Dodger Stadium. There could be some surprises in store, especially on the bul
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers completed their sweep over the San Francisco Giants on Sunday in extra innings. It was their sixth time reaching the century-mark during the last decade, which is better than any American League team and second only to the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League.
The Dodgers now have four days to game plan before they take on either the Philadelphia Phillies or the Atlanta Braves in the NLDS at Dodger Stadium.
There could be some surprises in store, especially on the bullpen front. Blake Treinen's season just ended with a shoulder issue, Edwin Díaz has enjoyed a resurgence since coming off the IL, Edgardo Henriquez is trending toward availability, and they still need to figure out the Roki Sasaki of it all.
But fans saw all of that coming. The more interesting roster development in the last week has been the battle of the No. 1 prospects: Josue De Paula vs. Dalton Rushing.
De Paula was optioned back to Triple-A after Shohei Ohtani came off the IL, and Rushing was officially reactivated from the IL ahead of the Giants series. De Paula, however, looks like he still has the upper hand here, and will be in LA during the bye week as the Dodgers consider all of their options.
Josue De Paula is on track to win Dodgers' postseason roster battle
The Dodgers are currently carrying three catchers: Rushing, Will Smith, and Hunter Feduccia. Whoever LA chooses to be the backup catcher, that player will be playing second fiddle to Smith (even more than they already do).
Last year, Ben Rortvedt started two games in the NL Wild Card Series while Smith came back from an injury, but he didn't make an appearance past Game 2 of the NLDS. Feduccia, though more dispensable than Rushing in most contexts, makes more sense in that role.
LA wants a big lefty bat they can keep on the bench, and De Paula established himself as the better bet almost immediately. At the same time, Rushing had the disadvantage of being on the IL, unable to state his own case.
The question is how the Dodgers will petition the Commissioner's Office to carry De Paula on the roster. He'll have to replace an injured player who's already served the minimum amount of time on the IL. In bringing Rushing back, the Dodgers needlessly complicated things.
But no doubt Andrew Friedman will figure it out. De Paula might only get a precious few at-bats throughout the month, but they clearly already trust him.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: Dodgers don't have a designated playoff closer. That isn't as bad as it sounds
item.dc:creator: Bill Shaikin
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott. - Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon. SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win t
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott.
- Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon.
SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win three consecutive World Series championships since the New York Yankees, from 1998 to 2000.
Those Yankees had a Hall of Fame closer. In 1998, Mariano Rivera got the final four outs of the clincher. In 1999, he got the final four outs. In 2000, he got the final three outs.
These Dodgers? Their closer? Your guess is as good as theirs.
“I do not know,” said Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations.
This might be a good time to know, no? The regular season is over. The postseason is upon us.
Alex Call hits a run-scoring double and Andy Pages follows with a three-run home run in the 10th inning of the Dodgers’ 5-1 win over the San Francisco Giants.
“I feel very confident that we’re going to be going into October with arguably the deepest and best pitching staff that we’ve had,” he said. “Exactly what their roles will be and how things will be ordered, I don’t know right now.”
Perhaps the Dodgers are overthinking this. They have done that before.
Tanner Scott converted 25 of 29 save opportunities this season, including saves Friday and Saturday.
But the strongest hitters on the Dodgers’ possible division series opponents are left-handed — Matt Olson, Drake Baldwin and Michael Harris II on the Atlanta Braves; Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber on the Philadelphia Phillies — and the Dodgers may not hesitate to use the left-handed Scott against those guys in the seventh or eighth inning.
In theory, these Dodgers have three candidates as closer: Scott, their marquee closer signing for 2025 and actual closer for most of 2026; Edwin Díaz, their marquee closer signing for 2026; and Roki Sasaki, their accidental closer last October.
Yet Friedman said he could envision scenarios where Evan Phillips could close, or even Brock Stewart, or perhaps Alex Vesia against a run of left-handed hitters. The Dodgers hope to activate Edgardo Henriquez for the playoffs. The starters could close, too, especially a well-rested Tyler Glasnow early in the first round.
Dave Roberts know the Dodgers’ chances of a three-peat rest on a surprise hero giving the team a timely boost. Meet Bill Plaschke’s top candidates for the job.
“We’ve got a number of guys that we really trust,” Friedman said. “Depending on who we’re playing, how deep our starter goes, there are a lot of factors that would go into it. But, more than who will be that pitcher on the mound, is the fact that we have so many candidates we feel really good about.”
That the Dodgers have improvised an October relief corps, transformed a rookie starter into a postseason closer and run bullpen games in elimination games might lead you to conclude Friedman does not really believe in the concept of a designated closer. In a world where “high leverage” is the trendy jargon, maybe a closer is more of an anachronism than a necessity.
That the Dodgers invested $72 million in Scott and $69 million in Díaz in consecutive winters would lead you to conclude Friedman does indeed believe in the concept of a designated closer. In fact, he does.
“I think it’s extremely helpful,” he said.
The Dodgers do not hold splashy news conferences to introduce closer candidates. When the Dodgers introduced Díaz last December, Friedman proudly introduced the three-time All-Star as the closer.
“For us, we have a high bar,” Friedman said then. “To name someone the closer, you have to be one of the best. You have to be elite and dominant at what you do.”
Díaz’s season went awry, limited to 18⅔ innings after elbow surgery and then a neck injury. But in five September appearances since his activation from the injured list, he gave up no runs and one hit in five innings, striking out nine of the 17 batters he faced. (In the same span, Scott has given up no runs and two hits in five innings, striking out nine of the 19 batters he faced.)
“What we’ve seen out of Díaz recently has been really encouraging,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “What that ultimately means, we don’t know yet.
“Of course, if you have a reliever who is really hot in October, that can be extremely valuable. It doesn’t mean you use him exclusively in the ninth. But, by and large, that’s how you would use him.”
Roberts saluted Díaz for working hard to get back to an uncertain assignment.
“I’m really proud of Edwin, given the deal he signed, to work it out, to go to the minors, to come back and pitch in whatever role we ask of him, that shows a lot of character,” Roberts said.
“He could have mailed this year in. That’s something that has not gone unnoticed. And we’ll see how October plays out.”
The Dodgers could be forgiven for believing it will all work out in the end. Their final pitcher in each of the World Series clinchers under Friedman, all starters: Julio Urías in 2020, Walker Buehler in 2024, Yoshinobu Yamamoto in 2025.
The pitchers to record a postseason save in those championship seasons: Kenley Jansen, Joe Kelly, Brusdar Graterol, Blake Treinen and Urias in 2020; Alex Vesia, Treinen and Buehler in 2024; Glasnow, Sasaki and Treinen in 2025.
The organizational flexibility can lead to some uncomfortable discussions within the clubhouse, as Roberts and coaches keep the relievers updated on the latest plan for how they might be used.
“It is tricky,” Roberts said. “These are constant conversations. They are ever-evolving. They are ongoing.”
If all goes right for the Dodgers, those conversations will be ongoing for another month.

item.title: [Orange County Register] Dodgers complete 100-win season with win over Giants
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

The Dodgers reached the end of the compulsory phase of their year, finishing the regular season with a 5-1 win in 10 innings against the San Francisco Giants on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park. The win was the Dodgers’ 100th of the season. It is the 12th time in franchise history that they have finished a season with 100 wins (including six of the past nine full seasons). None of the previous 100-win regular seasons were follo
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO – Well, enough of that – now on to the important stuff.
The Dodgers reached the end of the compulsory phase of their year, finishing the regular season with a 5-1 win in 10 innings against the San Francisco Giants on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park.
The win was the Dodgers’ 100th of the season. It is the 12th time in franchise history that they have finished a season with 100 wins (including six of the past nine full seasons). None of the previous 100-win regular seasons were followed by a World Series championship.
The Dodgers will now take Monday off before getting together for four days of simulated games, live batting practice and whatever else they deem necessary to get ready for the opening of the postseason that will determine if they can become the first National League franchise to win three consecutive World Series championships.
Game 1 of their NL Division Series will be Saturday at Dodger Stadium against the winner of the Wild Card Series between the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies. That best-of-three series begins Tuesday in Atlanta – and the Dodgers will be watching.
“There’s going to be some watch parties at the ballpark. I thought that was something that was really good,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of the bye week itinerary established in 2024. “You’re not playing in the Wild Card Series, but you’re watching it and you kind of get your juices going. There’s also a bonding piece that I think is important.
“I thought we did a good job of having enough live and game situations, simulating them. Our coaches are sort of revisiting what we did a couple years ago. If there’s things we want to improve on or what – it worked out well a couple years ago. A lot of it’s also contingent on how guys are feeling, making sure they get rested and reset.”
MLB’s easiest September schedule allowed the Dodgers to go into their bye week with positive momentum. They went 18-7 in the final month (including 6-0 against the Giants in the final 10 days). Only the San Diego Padres (19-6) had more wins in the month.
Those bye-week sim games essentially started this weekend at Oracle Park.
On Sunday, the Dodgers sent seven pitchers to the mound to get their work. They allowed one run on five hits — and survived giving up the potential game-deciding home run. Giants shortstop Christian Koss took Dodgers reliever Bobby Miller deep leading off the eighth inning — but replay review turned the home run into a foul ball.
Roki Sasaki made his third appearance out of the bullpen since returning from a blister and did nothing to undermine his status as perhaps the most important bullpen weapon the Dodgers will have this postseason. He struck out two of the three batters he faced in a 1-2-3 inning.
Over his three innings in relief, Sasaki has faced 11 batters and struck out six, allowing two hits in his first appearance and none since.
“I think the fastball’s better,” Roberts said, comparing the version of Sasaki the Dodgers got when they moved him to the bullpen last postseason. “I think the split’s better. It’s also nice that he’s already done it. Just in total, he’s just a better pitcher than he was last year and a lot more confident.”
Edwin Diaz continued to affirm his status as a rediscovered bullpen weapon with another 1-2-3 inning. And Roberts reported Edgardo Henriquez has been throwing bullpen sessions this weekend and will participate in the bye week workouts with the expectation that he will be ready to return from his lower back injury and be part of the Dodgers’ NLDS bullpen.
The Dodgers’ offense didn’t spark to life until the 10th inning when Alex Call doubled in the free runner then trotted home on a three-run home run by Andy Pages.

item.content:encoded:
For nine-plus innings, the Dodgers and Giants couldn’t buy a hit with a runner in scoring position, but in the tenth, the Dodgers broke through for a 5-1 win. Alex Call and Andy Pages recorded two-out hits, a double, and a three-run shot to give the Dodgers their first lead in this game and the only one they’d need.
Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants
Making a habit out of squandering chances through nine innings, the Dodgers scored four in extras to beat the Giants
Before getting to that point of being tied in extras, Jack Dreyer did a reasonable job of keeping the Giants at bay as an opener, but a stolen base allowed the opportunity for just a pair of singles to open the scoring in the second. Shay Whitcomb singled and stole second, later driven in by Scott Bandura—his first RBI of the season, playing in just his 13th big league game. Bandura also tried to steal a base, but this time Dreyer was alert to the danger and picked him off.
Facing a traditional bullpen game with Carson Seymour completing just one inning to open this one, the Dodgers first threatened to score in the third, the inning marked by Tony Vitello’s ejection. With two on and a 2-2 count to Mookie Betts, a check swing in which he probably went around was called a no-swing. Vitello came out to argue what had already been a topic of frustration earlier in the game and was thrown out for the seventh time in his 2026. The Giants, however, got out of the jam, as Betts struck out on the next pitch, and Sam Hentges also punched out Freddie Freeman.
What the Dodgers offense couldn’t do in the third, it did in the following frame. Kyle Tucker got on to leadoff the inning thanks to a defensive error by the second baseman and moved to third on a Max Muncy double—his 27th of the season, setting a new career high in a single season. With two on and one out, Andy Pages evened the score with a sacrifice fly.
Through the following innings, the Dodgers kept threatening but never coming through, first with a Freddie Freeman hit with a man on being taken away by a great defensive play from Jonah Cox—somewhat redeeming himself for the error that contributed to the Dodgers’ first run. That, by the way, would be Freeman’s last action in the game, replaced after five by Kiké Hernández as Dave Roberts rotated key pieces.
In the sixth, Muncy nearly wrote another chapter in his book as a giant killer. But the deepest part of the park was just deep enough to keep him from a solo shot in a ball that would’ve gone out in 23 of 30 stadiums. Perhaps the biggest squandered chance, though, came in the seventh and eighth when the Dodgers first stranded a leadoff double by Tommy Edman with three straight groundouts—an inning later, after Muncy secured his third hit of the day, Andy Pages hit into an inning-ending double play with two on and one out.
The Dodgers’ pitching was the reason the offense kept getting these opportunities to take the lead. Justin Wrobleski was the first pitcher out of the bullpen for the Dodgers, but looking for an even distribution of workload, he only completed two scoreless innings in under 30 pitches. Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz combined to strike out three, each with a scoreless frame.
Although Wrobleski had a couple of scares, the Giants truly came back to threaten again in the seventh when Bobby Miller took the mound, but also without actually breaking through. With runners at the corners and no outs, Miller secured a strikeout, then lucked into Marcelo Mayer staying at third on a wild pitch quickly recovered by Hunter Feduccia, recorded another punchout, and finished off the inning with a groundout.
With both teams exhausting new ways of threatening without actually scoring, the Giants looked like they’d take the lead with a leadoff bomb in the eighth by Christian Koss. However, the call on the field of a home run was overturned when replay made it clear it was a foul ball, and the score remained 1-1 through nine innings.
Even in the tenth, it looked like the Dodgers were going to strand the ghost runner after their first two hitters were retired without him advancing to third, but Call came through, and an intentional walk later, Pages had the big hit of the game. With the four RBI he recorded in this game, Pages left Ohtani behind and isolated himself as the Dodgers’ RBI leader this season, with 85.
Sunday particulars
Home run: Andy Pages (23)
WP —Alex Vesia (3-1): 1 IP, 1 hit, 1 strikeout
LP —Duncan Davitt (0-1):1 IP, 2 hits, 4 runs, 3 earned runs, 1 walk
Up next
The Dodgers get a little under a week off before they get back on the field on Saturday at home. They’ll be playing host to the winner of the Wild Card round between the Braves and Phillies in game 1 of the NLDS. No starters have been announced for that series.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Roki Sasaki delivered another impressive relief outing against the San Francisco Giants in his new role.
Sasaki the dominant reliever
Roki Sasaki pitched a clean inning on Friday, September 25th, recording two strikeouts and allowing no hits or walks.
Sasaki needed just 14 pitches to get through the order. His pitches all came in at a higher velocity than his season average.
His fastball stood out, averaging 100 mph, 2.2 mph above his season average; his splitter was 1.7 mph up, and his slider was 0.4 mph up as well, according to Baseball Savant.
He got two whiffs and three called strikes. More importantly, the horizontal break on all of his pitches was higher than average, and his slider got some extra vertical induced.
This was only Sasaki’s second outing in 2026 as a reliever, a role he has assumed since returning from the injured list after a blister on his middle finger.
His first outing was on Tuesday, September 22nd, when Sasaki allowed two hits but stranded both baserunners with two strikeouts.
Dave Roberts is impressed with Sasaki
After Friday’s game, manager Dave Roberts noted how dominant Sasaki is pitching in his new role.
“I think the fastball is better. I think the split’s better. And it’s also nice that he’s already done it,” Roberts said.
“Just in total, he’s just a better pitcher than he was last year and a lot more confident. And certainly the stuff was really good the last couple of outings.”
As a right-handed arm, Sasaki has established himself as a trustworthy arm, whether in the bullpen or the starting rotation.
He was the postseason closer last year, but with the rise of Tanner Scott and Edgardo Henriquez, along with the surprise emergence of Edwin Diaz, Sasaki will not be relied on as much as the bullpen trust tree grows.
“I think it’s just better to have as many guys that you have confidence in and leverage. It just allows us to deploy guys whenever we need to. I feel comfortable with a lot of guys at the back end for sure,” Roberts added.
Whether he comes in during the seventh, eighth, or ninth inning, Sasaki is no longer a question mark, and he pitches like an exclamation point.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Edwin Díaz Feeling Like Himself Again as Postseason Approaches
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Edwin Díaz‘s late-season resurgence continued Thursday night, as the Dodgers reliever delivered another impressive outing in the team’s 4-2 loss to the Padres. Díaz worked a scoreless ninth inning, striking out two batters and providing another encouraging sign that he may be finding his form at exactly the right time.
After a frustrating season that included a stint in Triple-A to work on his mechanics, Díaz believes his pitches are finally behaving the way he wants them to. And with the Dodgers preparing for October, the veteran reliever is eager to demonstrate that he belongs in their postseason bullpen.
“I was throwing strikes. That’s my goal, throwing strikes,” Díaz said after the game. “If I throw strikes, my pitches will play up. And I think today I was throwing strike one, and then I was trying to make them chase.”
A Breakthrough That Started in Triple-A
Díaz credited his recent improvement to a mechanical adjustment he made during his final days in Triple-A. After a particularly productive bullpen session, he felt so encouraged that he asked to pitch the following day.
“I threw a nice bullpen in Triple-A, and the next day I told them, ‘I want to pitch today. I want to pitch the next day because I feel really good,'” Díaz recalled.
“I think that helped me to set my mind, to set everything. Have a good outing before I came here and keep having good outings is what I want.”
The results have carried over into his appearances with the Dodgers, where he feels increasingly comfortable with his delivery and pitch execution.
“As soon as it clicked, I was feeling good in my last outing in Triple-A,” he explained. “As soon as I got here, I kept working, and everything is playing really good for me right now. I’m really happy. Just got to finish the season strong and have a good postseason.”
His slider was particularly effective Thursday, generating plenty of swings at pitches outside the strike zone.
“I think today was my shape, but the slider was really good,” Díaz said. “It had a lot of break, and they were chasing by far. So that was really good.”
Experience Helped Him Through the Struggles
Asked whether he ever worried about failing to rediscover his mechanics before the end of the season, Díaz said he never allowed himself to think that way.
“I never thought about that. I was trying to figure out how to get back. I was putting a lot of work together, but I never thought, ‘Oh, I miss everything.'”
“I was just trying to hustle and get better, try to get better, try to get better. Because I knew when my pitches are on the spot where I want, everything plays out. So now I can do whatever I want.”
Díaz believes his years of major league experience helped him maintain that mindset during the difficult stretches.
“Having a lot of time in the league helped me a lot on that,” he said. “Maybe if I was a young guy, maybe I would try to overthink. But I know I’ve been in the league for so long, and I know how to make adjustments.”
That experience has allowed him to concentrate on the work rather than becoming consumed by disappointing results.
Ready to Prove He Belongs in October
With the Dodgers having secured their first-round bye, the remaining regular-season games offer Díaz an opportunity to continue building momentum and make his case for a spot on the NLDS roster.
Asked directly whether he believes he has demonstrated that he belongs in the postseason bullpen, Díaz emphasized that his focus remains on delivering results whenever his number is called.
“Right now, I’m just trying to do my job,” he said. “I just want to put up zeroes when they give me the ball. I’m ready to pitch every day.”
“I just want them to keep trusting me and keep giving me the ball, just to show them I’m ready to pitch in the postseason.”
And when a reporter followed up by asking whether he trusts himself, Díaz didn’t hesitate.
“Oh, 100%. Always.”
For a Dodgers bullpen that has endured its share of uncertainty this season, Díaz’s recent performances are a welcome development. His confidence appears to be returning alongside his command, and Thursday’s outing offered another indication that the veteran right-hander intends to make himself part of the team’s October plans.

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers dropped the rubber match of their series against the San Diego Padres on Thursday, falling 4-2 in their regular season home finale at Dodger Stadium.
In the ninth inning, something encouraging happened. Edwin Diaz took the mound and shut the door.
The right-hander struck out two batters and allowed no hits in a clean ninth. After the game, manager Dave Roberts offered a notable assessment of where Diaz stands heading into October.
Roberts on Diaz’s Recent Run
Roberts has watched Diaz closely since returning from the injured list. Each outing has looked better than the last.
“This has been the best of the 4,” Roberts said of Diaz’s performance. “He’ll pitch 1 of the games this weekend, 7th, 8th or 9th.”
Diaz kept it simple when asked what has been working.
“I was throwing strikes,” Diaz said. “That’s my goal.”
The Road Back for Diaz
Diaz’s 2026 season nearly ended before it began. He underwent surgery in late April to remove loose bodies from his right elbow, an injury that put him on the 60-day injured list and cast doubt on whether he would pitch again this year.
His early-season numbers before the surgery were ugly. But the version of Diaz that has returned looks far closer to the pitcher who posted a 1.63 ERA with a 0.87 WHIP for the New York Mets in 2025, ranking second among qualified relievers with a 38 percent strikeout rate.
The Dodgers signed Diaz knowing his ceiling. Getting that ceiling back in September, right before October, changes the complexion of their bullpen.
Final Word for the Dodgers
Edwin Diaz came to Los Angeles to close games in October. Elbow surgery and a lost summer threatened to erase that plan entirely.
Now, the plan is back. Roberts is giving him the ball in the seventh, eighth, or ninth. The strikeouts are coming. The strikes are landing.
The Dodgers’ postseason is approaching. Diaz intends to be a factor. Based on what Roberts said Thursday, the Dodgers believe him.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Tyler Glasnow walked off the mound Thursday night having done almost everything the Dodgers could have asked of him.
The result, however, belonged to the Padres.
Glasnow carried a no-hit bid into the sixth inning and struck out 11 over 6⅓ innings in his final tune-up before the postseason, but the Padres broke through late and held on to beat the Dodgers, 4-2, in the final home game of the 2026 regular season at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers finished the night 97-62, having already secured a first-round bye earlier Thursday. The Padres, meanwhile, clinched a postseason berth and will play in a Wild Card Series.
And with the postseason bracket beginning to take shape, there is a very real possibility these two teams could be back here in nine days.
For six innings, though, Glasnow looked every bit like a pitcher the Dodgers will want leading their rotation into October.
Ethan Salas broke up the no-hitter with a one-out single in the sixth. Salas eventually scored on a sacrifice fly, and two more singles helped the Padres add to its lead.
Glasnow entered the inning with the Dodgers still searching for their first run. He left it with the Padres ahead.
His final line was as sharp as the circumstances allowed: 6⅓ innings, three hits, three runs, all earned, two walks and 11 strikeouts on 91 pitches, 58 for strikes.
“I feel like I'm in a pretty good rhythm right now, so it's perfect time to bring it in to the postseason,” Glasnow said afterward.
The 11 strikeouts came on 79 pitches before he returned for the seventh, and the outing offered another encouraging sign for a Dodgers rotation preparing for the most important games of the season.
The Dodgers had opportunities against the Padres but repeatedly failed to capitalize, stranding seven runners through the middle innings.
Mookie Betts, meanwhile, continued to do what he has done all season: reach base.
Betts reached safely in all four plate appearances, going 3-for-4 with a double, two singles and a walk.
Shohei Ohtani also collected two hits, including an RBI double in the ninth inning that brought the Dodgers within two runs. Ohtani's late hit gave the Dodgers one final spark, but the Padres closed the door to finish off the regular-season home finale.
Dave Roberts said he has liked what he has seen from Ohtani over the past two games.
“The last 2 nights, he’s looked great,” Roberts said.
The Dodgers' final home game also provided another encouraging glimpse of Edwin Díaz.
Díaz worked a scoreless ninth, allowing no hits and striking out two on just 11 pitches. Since returning from the injured list, he has thrown four scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk while striking out eight.
Over his last four appearances, opponents are 1-for-13 with eight strikeouts.
Díaz said his slider is in its best shape right now, a development that comes at an important time as he tries to earn a spot on the Dodgers' postseason roster.
“I'm trying just to do my job. I'm just gonna wanna put zeros when they give me the ball,” Díaz said. “I'm ready to pitch every day. I just want them to keep trusting me and keep giving me the ball just to show them I'm ready to pitch in the postseason.”
Roberts called Thursday Díaz's best performance of his four appearances since returning.
“This has been the best of the four,” Roberts said.
There are only three regular-season games remaining, but the Dodgers have already accomplished one of their primary objectives. The first-round bye is secured. The home schedule is finished. Now comes the final push toward October.
The loss also did little to concern Roberts about the Dodgers' record against winning teams during the second half.
“I don’t think so, I don’t put stock into it,” Roberts said. “Once you get to the postseason, it’s a different game.”
That is the challenge waiting for the Dodgers.
Thursday was less about the standings than it was about getting their pieces in place. Glasnow looked in rhythm. Díaz continued to build momentum. Ohtani looked sharp at the plate. Betts reached base four times.
The Padres, meanwhile, celebrated a postseason berth in the visiting clubhouse.
There is still baseball to be played before October arrives. But with the Dodgers holding a bye and the Padres headed for the Wild Card round, Thursday's matchup may have offered a preview of a game that matters much more.
“We’re gonna have an exciting postseason, so just ride with us,” Roberts said.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Dodgers clinch No. 2 seed and important playoff bye despite loss to Padres
item.dc:creator: Kevin Baxter
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The Dodgers clinched the National League’s No. 2 seed and a first-round playoff bye, gaining five crucial days to rest a battered roster before their Oct. 3 NLDS opener. - The Dodgers lose to the San Diego Padres 4-2 and drop the three-game series despite Tyler Glasnow carrying a no-hitter into the sixth inning. - The Padres clinched a postseason berth as the Dodgers prepare for their final regular-season series in San Francisco after drawing more
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers clinched the National League’s No. 2 seed and a first-round playoff bye, gaining five crucial days to rest a battered roster before their Oct. 3 NLDS opener.
- The Dodgers lose to the San Diego Padres 4-2 and drop the three-game series despite Tyler Glasnow carrying a no-hitter into the sixth inning.
- The Padres clinched a postseason berth as the Dodgers prepare for their final regular-season series in San Francisco after drawing more than 4 million fans to Dodger Stadium this season.
The Dodgers didn’t win Thursday. But they got something far more valuable before they even took the field for their 4-2 loss to the San Diego Padres.
With the Atlanta Braves’ loss to the Cincinnati Reds earlier in the day, the Dodgers clinched the second seed in the National League playoffs and the first-round bye that goes with it. That means the Dodgers will get five days off next week to prepare for their playoff opener, a godsend for a bruised and bloodied team that has stumbled to the finish of the regular season.
“I think we all know why it’s important,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said of the break. “There’s a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here, a lot of aches and pains this year.”
For the Padres (89-70), the victory was important because it clinched a wild-card berth and a franchise-record third consecutive trip to the postseason.
In addition to Freeman, who has been hobbled all month by a sore right knee, the Dodgers are rushing to get designated hitter Shohei Ohtani and closer Edwin Díaz healthy. Both had big games Thursday with Ohtani going two for five with a run batted in, the first time he’s had multiple hits or an RBI in more than a month. Díaz, meanwhile, pitched a perfect ninth, striking out two.
Other players also are getting healthy. Center fielder Andy Pages, who missed a month with a broken hand, returned to the lineup three days ago. Dalton Rushing, who is competing for a bench spot on the postseason roster, is expected to be activated off the injured list Friday. Left-hander Blake Snell, who came out of his last start nine days ago after just an inning, will make his final postseason tuneup Saturday.
All of them will benefit from some additional rest before their playoff opener, at Dodger Stadium, on Oct. 3.
And speaking of Dodger Stadium, the No. 2 playoff seed carries another important perk: the home-field advantage for the Division Series — and possibly the World Series, if the Dodgers make it that far. Home has certainly been an advantage for the Dodgers, who drew a sellout crowd of 53,027 Thursday, pushing the team’s total home attendance over 4 million for the second straight year.
“It’s more turning of the turnstiles than any venue in the world,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “The amazing thing is that it’s not just localized. It’s international. Everyone looks different at Dodger Stadium.
“It’s spectacular and our players certainly feed off of it.”
The Dodgers are one of five franchises in big-league history to draw more than 4 million fans in a season but just two others — the Toronto Blue Jays, from 1991-93, and the New York Yankees, in the final four years at old Yankee Stadium — did it in consecutive seasons.
And the Dodgers are the only team to do it since 2008. They also lead the majors in road attendance this season, having drawn 2.82 million, or 36,159 a game. For some fans, it’s hard to separate their support from the team’s success.
“A synergy exists between we the fans and the players,” said Charles Flores, an associate professor at Cal State L.A. and lifelong Dodgers fan who attended more than a dozen games this season. “One inspires the other.”
Russ Hoffman of Santa Clarita, a season-ticket holder for 40 years, agrees.
“The atmosphere created by drawing so many fans definitely contributes to their success,” he said. “Winning continuously drives the attendance and the current ownership has committed the assets to do that.”
That edge can be even bigger in the playoffs. The Dodgers lost just five of 16 postseason games at home — a .688 winning percentage — en route to World Series titles the last two years.
“During the playoffs, Dodger Stadium is a tough place to play because it’s 56,000 crazed fans yelling on every play,” said Stan Brooks, an award-winning film producer and longtime season-ticket holder. “The fans are so loud and the environment is so intense every night.”
The Dodgers (97-62) will finish the regular season with three games this weekend in San Francisco, where they will continue their preparation for the postseason.
In the final home game of the regular season Mookie Betts, dropped to second in the lineup with Ohtani’s return, went three for four with a walk, raising his average for September to .367, while Freeman had two hits for the third time in four games.
“I’m just encouraged with Shohei getting a couple hits, Mookie staying hot. That’s what it’s all about,” Freeman said. “Getting hot right now.
“That’s all we were looking forward to this last week is getting our guys back on the field.”
That didn’t add up to much offense Thursday, with the Dodgers stranding eight runners and going 0 for 8 with men in scoring position through eight innings. They avoided their first shutout of the season at home on Adrian Morejon’s balk in the eighth before Ohtani doubled in the second run with two outs in the ninth.
For the past 17 years, Chaz Perea and his four-person crew have been responsible for every bit of stadium landscaping that isn’t the field itself.
On the mound, Tyler Glasnow, who will be the Dodgers’ fourth starter in the postseason, was perfect through three innings. He walked Fernando Tatis Jr. on four pitches to start the fourth but didn’t allow another Padres batter to reach base until Ethan Salas singled with one out in the sixth.
That proved costly when Tatis singled on the next pitch, sending Salas to third, from where he scored on Dustin Harris’ sacrifice fly, putting the Padres ahead to stay.
Glasnow (5-2) got out of the inning by striking out Manny Machado, giving him a season-high 11 strikeouts and 21 in his last two starts. But San Diego then blew the game open in the seventh, chasing Glasnow and scoring three times off reliever Justin Wrobleski on run-scoring singles by Austin Hayes, Salas and Tatis.
Staff writer Maddie Lee contributed to this report.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Edgardo Henriquez Makes Big Stride in Race to Return for NLDS
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez provided an update on his back injury, which has him on the injured list and makes his postseason status uncertain. Edgardo Henriquez’s injury progress Henriquez told The Athletic’s Fabian Aradaya that he threw a bullpen session on Wednesday, September 24th, his first since being placed on the injured list. item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez provided an update on his back injury, which has him on the injured list and makes his postseason status uncertain.
Edgardo Henriquez’s injury progress
Henriquez told The Athletic’s Fabian Aradaya that he threw a bullpen session on Wednesday, September 24th, his first since being placed on the injured list.
He feels like his back is in a better spot, and that he can get ready for the National League Division Series on Saturday, October 3rd.
The Dodgers put Henriquez on the 15-day injured list a little more than a week ago with a low-grade back strain, manager Dave Roberts revealed.
When he placed Henriquez on the injured list, Roberts was “hopeful” Henriquez would be back for the postseason.
The MRI, according to him, was “positive,” all things considered.
Thus far, things have played out accordingly, though the next week of recovery and rest will be the big test.
Why the Dodgers need Henriquez
Henriquez is the Dodgers’ most impressive right-handed reliever out of the bullpen.
He has a 2.62 ERA and a 2.50 FIP, and his profile is ideal for postseason baseball. He misses the barrel of the bat, strikes out hitters, and limits home runs, with command being the determining factor in his outing go.
Luckily for the Dodgers, Henriquez has figured out his control well enough that it hasn’t been a problem this year.
Compared to Edwin Diaz, Henriquez is much more reliable, while Brock Stewart and Evan Phillips are better suited for middle-relief chances.
If healthy, Henriquez should get save chances, with Roki Sasaki and Tanner Scott right in the mix as well. Diaz has started to creep up in the mix, but Henriquez has the confidence and demeanor to take command of the role.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] How much should Dodgers fans buy into Edwin Diaz’s success since coming off the IL?

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts did not mince his words when talking about Edwin Díaz during his mid-September rehab assignment. "He needs to pitch better. It hasn't been good," said Roberts.
Diaz, who has the highest average annual value in MLB relief pitcher history ($23M), struggled in the first four appearances of his rehab assignment. He had thrown just 40 of 86 pitches for strikes in his first four games with Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Diaz's fourth appearance was especially worrying. He threw 30 pitches — just 13 of them for strikes — walked three batters and allowed five runs. Diaz rehab came in the Pacific Coast League, which is notorious for being the most hitter-friendly league in all of baseball. That atrocious outing came in Sugar Land, however, which is the most pitcher-friendly venue in the PCL.
When the Dodgers activated Diaz from the injured list, Roberts revealed he'd be used in low-leverage situations. Well, he has been perfectly fine in his three low-leverage outings since September 18, which has assuaged some of the Dodgers fans panic levels.
Should Dodgers fans buy into Edwin Diaz’s success?
Diaz has only allowed one hit since returning from the IL. The Dodgers, however, had a run margin of +19 in those three games.
“The way he’s throwing, the ninth is possible, yes,” said Roberts after the Dodgers 7-0 win over the Padres on September 22.
The Dodgers will almost certainly give Diaz another opportunity against the San Diego Padres on Thursday. The current home series against the Friars will be Diaz's last opportunity to pitch against a playoff team before the postseason begins.
The Dodgers are currently without Emmet Sheehan, Edgardo Henriquez, Will Klein, and Eric Lauer. Outside of Alex Vesia, the rest of the bullpen is incredibly shaky. Tanner Scott has a 5.40 ERA so far this month, Justin Wrobleski has not improved since being moved to the bullpen, and who knows what Blake Treinen has left in the tank?
Dodgers fans should get accustomed to seeing Diaz the rest of the season. He's quite possibly the linchpin to this team going deep in the playoffs with the way this bullpen looks right now. Dodgers fans have the right to remain skeptical that Diaz will return to the optimal version of himself,

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers Considering Edwin Diaz for Postseason Closer Despite Disastrous Season
item.dc:creator: Gabe Smallson; Unknown
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have countless questions to address before the postseason as their quest to win three consecutive championships continues, but one of the biggest uncertainties on the roster is relief pitcher Edwin Díaz. Díaz is a three-time All-Star and has an impressive reputation on the mound. He and his 253 saves through his first nine seasons in MLB earned a massive three-year, $69 million contract to help the Dodgers towards their ultimate goal. The start to his Dodgers career was f
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have countless questions to address before the postseason as their quest to win three consecutive championships continues, but one of the biggest uncertainties on the roster is relief pitcher Edwin Díaz.
Díaz is a three-time All-Star and has an impressive reputation on the mound. He and his 253 saves through his first nine seasons in MLB earned a massive three-year, $69 million contract to help the Dodgers towards their ultimate goal.
The start to his Dodgers career was far from ideal to say the least, pushing a 10.50 ERA through his first seven appearances (six innings). Towards the end of April, he was placed on the injured list as he underwent a procedure to remove loose bodies in his elbow.
Upon his return in late-July, it was unforunately more of the same with 11 earned runs in nine appearances. After heading back to the injured list for a month with neck inflammation, he has appeared to make significant strides with just one hit and walk allowed to go along with six strikeouts in his last three outings.
Manager Dave Roberts knows that the timing couldn't be worse given the imminent postseason and Díaz needing more reps, but at least for the moment, the skipper sees someone who can pitch in October in Díaz.
“I think it’s one of those things where if you’re one of the 12 pitchers on a postseason roster, you’re in the ‘trust tree’” Roberts said. “He’s put himself right smack in that conversation. Given all that he’s had to go through this year to right the ship is a big credit to him.”
Roberts also admitted that reasons beyond Díaz's control may seem to have influenced his poor play to start his Dodgers tenure, but perhaps these are all in the rear-view for the reliever.
“I think he’s in as good a spot as he’s been in all year, mentally, physically. The ball is coming out well,” Roberts said. “Yeah, I think that swagger is starting to come back, and I like the way that the energy that he’s exuding, it’s real. It’s something for us to build on.”
Roberts still couldn't put a label on who will have the 'closer' role come the postseason, but detailed a plan for a different pitcher who saw immense struggles to start the Dodgers chapter of his career (Tanner Scott) and how the two can work in tandem down the stretch.
“In a perfect world, as we all know the world’s not perfect, I would love [a set closer],” Roberts said. “I think if there’s an opportunity, for example, for Tanner [Scott] to pitch a high-leverage inning in the seventh or the eighth inning, it’s just hard to pass that up if he’s the best option right there. Because you just don’t know where the ninth inning is going to be.
“Those are things that you have to kind of toil with, and those are always good things for people to debate. Right now I don’t see a one-person closer.”
Sign up for our free newsletter and follow us on X/Twitter and Facebook for the latest news.
Gabe Smallson is a sportswriter based in Los Angeles with a focus in sports and entertainment content. Gabe has previously worked at Newsweek and Dodgers Nation. He graduated from San Francisco State University in 2020 and received his Masters of Science at the University of Southern California in 2025.

item.title: [truebluela.com] Dodgers notes: Postseason bullpen in a good spot
item.dc:creator: Andy Lane Chapman
item.description: Tuesday night’s game against the San Diego Padres was reminiscent of the 2024 playoffs when the Dodgers were forced to employ a bullpen in the NLDS to keep their playoff hopes alive against those same Padres. Both outcomes were the same, with the bullpen shutting down the Friars and getting a big win. That postseason saw a lot of bullpen usage, and in this one the Dodgers are stacked with starters. Still, the bullpen is always a big part of the postseason. As Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic points
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday night’s game against the San Diego Padres was reminiscent of the 2024 playoffs when the Dodgers were forced to employ a bullpen in the NLDS to keep their playoff hopes alive against those same Padres. Both outcomes were the same, with the bullpen shutting down the Friars and getting a big win.
That postseason saw a lot of bullpen usage, and in this one the Dodgers are stacked with starters. Still, the bullpen is always a big part of the postseason.
As Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic points out, 41 days ago manager Dave Roberts was asking the media what choices did he truly have to deploy in the ninth inning of games. Now, he could have several options.
Edwin Diaz, the closer they paid handsomely in the offseason, has not had a great season. He’s been on the IL twice and had an era over 11.00 at one point this summer. But since returning from his latest IL stint, he has faced 11 batters, struck out six and only allowed two to reach base.
“I think it’s one of those things where if you’re one of the 12 pitchers on a postseason roster, you’re in the trust tree,” Roberts said “He’s put himself right smack in that conversation. Given all that he’s had to go through this year to right the ship is a big credit to him.”
Roki Sasaki is also someone who will be in the mix for the ninth inning spot. He has also just returned from his own IL stint, pitching with dermabond on his blister. He allowed two singles, but worked around them for a scoreless inning in Tuesday night’s game. He will appear in Friday night’s game as he continues to work towards a spot in the bullpen that will likely vary as the postseason goes on.
Tanner Scott has been the Dodgers’ most reliable arm out of the bullpen this season, and Roberts has remarked how it would be nice to be able to use Scott in high leverage spots that may not come just in the ninth inning.
“I think if there’s an opportunity, for example, for Tanner to pitch a high-leverage inning in the seventh or the eighth inning, it’s just hard to pass that up if he’s the best option right there,” Roberts said. “You just don’t know where the ninth inning is going to be.”
Roberts also added that the team is sitting in their best position with regards to the bullpen as they have ever been. Evan Phillips and Brock Stewart round out the current options, and the team hopes that Edguardo Henriquez can recover from his back issues to appear in the playoffs. With the starters this team has overall this may be the best pitching staff the Dodgers have ever sent to the playoffs.

item.title: [sandiegouniontribune.com] Padres pregame: Jason Adam activated, Griffin Canning optioned ahead of Game 2 vs. Dodgers
