item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — A quad injury cost Jason Adam the chance to help the Padres in last year’s NL Wild Card Series. The team is intent on seeing what the 35-year-old veteran can provide this time around.
Out since late June with a shoulder injury, Adam was activated ahead of Wednesday’s 7:10 p.m. start at Dodger Stadium. To make room, right-hander Griffin Canning was optioned to Triple-A El Paso and reliever Alek Jacob was designated for assignment to allow Adam to rejoin the 40-man roster.
“We saw last year when he got hurt how much we missed him just within the team dynamic and what he provides as experience out there in the bullpen,” Padres manager Craig Stammen said. “We’ve got a lot more experience than what we had last year in the bullpen right now with those guys being together. But Jason’s a big part of that. He’s a big part of that group out there, and then he’s a pretty darn good pitcher also.”
A first-time All-Star last year, Adam allowed nine runs on seven hits and two walks over 1⅓ innings across three rehab appearances with El Paso. But both he and the team were satisfied with the stuff he showed in hitter-friendly conditions, as well as in live batting practice on Monday, and added his experience to a bullpen that was a strength last year and this year.
Adam’s velocity has trended down from about 95 mph the year the Padres acquired him in 2024 (1.95 ERA) to 94 mph last year (1.93 ERA) to 93 mph this year (2.51 ERA). He missed time earlier in the year as he returned from last year’s season-ending quad surgery and said Tuesday he was eager to get back in the thick of a postseason push.
“Yeah, I’d love to be part of every game,” Adam said after joining the team at Dodger Stadium on Tuesday. “What this team’s doing is really special. So I just want to fill my role, however that looks, and help them win ballgames. We’ve seen pretty well that this team’s good with or without me. I just want to do my part to contribute.”
Ousted from the rotation earlier this summer, Canning was better as a reliever (3.82 ERA in 35⅓ innings) than as a starter (6.79 ERA in 50 ⅓ innings) and had been critical in helping the team piece together games ahead of the trade deadline. But the team only needs three starters for the NL Wild Card Series, he was behind the likes of Robbie Ray, Casey Mize and Randy Vásquez in terms of depth arms for a short series and David Morgan has allowed one run in his last 7⅔ innings to seemingly cement his spot in the depth chart ahead of Canning.
The Padres optioning Canning to the minors means he cannot return to the active roster without an injury until the middle of the NL Division Series, after 15 days.
Jacob, 28, had a 5.58 ERA in 61⅓ innings at Triple-A El Paso and 4.18 ERA in 56 innings across parts of four seasons in the majors. He pitched in three games this year, allowing three runs in five innings as an up-and-down arm.
Ohtani returns, Salas starts
As expected the Dodgers reinstated Shohei Ohtani (biceps, knee from the injured list, as well as left-hander Tarik Skubal from the bereavement list. To make room, outfielder Josue De Paula and Hurt were optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Ohtani will bat second and serve as the designated hitter for the Dodgers, who have won eight of 11 so far against the Padres this year. Ohtani was 0-for-3 when he last played on Sept. 9 and was in a .122/.295/.184 slide over his last 13 games.
Tonight's #Dodgers lineup vs. Padres: pic.twitter.com/SyL3INJl9z
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 23, 2026
As for the Padres, Ethan Salas will get his first start at Dodger Stadium and second pairing with left-hander Robbie Ray. The only starter he has not worked with is Michael King.
Salas (.627 OPS) was 1-for-2 off the bench on Tuesday. He will bat ninth in a lineup that will see Samad Taylor (.856 OPS) get the start as the DH after Austin Hays did so on Tuesday.
Tonight’s lineup. pic.twitter.com/zLU04b89qh
— San Diego Padres (@Padres) September 23, 2026
While the Padres’ lead on the Diamondbacks was shaved from five to four games with five games left in the season — including three head-to-head matches in San Diego — Tuesday’s loss did little to diminish postseason odds, which are at 93.5% according to FanGraphs.com.
As was the case on Tuesday, any combination of two Padres wins and/or Diamondbacks losses will clinch the team’s third straight postseason berth.
Right-hander Merrill Kelly (9-14, 5.00 ERA) will start at Coors Field for Arizona against Rockies right-hander Mason Adams (0-1, 5.09 ERA). First pitch there is 5:40 p.m..
The Padres, Cubs and Phillies all began Wednesday with identical 87-70 records, although the Padres have to finish ahead of both teams to earn home games in the NL Wild Card Series as they lost both season series.
The Dodgers’ magic number to clinch a first-round bye over the Braves is 1. They are also one game ahead of the Brewers in the race for the NL’s No. 1 seed.
Glass half full
The Dodgers just about emptied the bullpen in Tuesday’s 7-0 win over the Padres. In the aftermath of another bullpen game slowing an offense that ranks first in the majors this month in OPS (.835), a half-glass-full view of what transpired was worth taking forward.
The Padres saw all but two relievers — Kris Bubic and Evan Phillips — in their first shutout loss since Aug. 25 and they still had two more games to wade through in Chavez Ravine.
“They’re really good bullpen arms, so the more you can see them, the better shot you have,” first baseman Ty France said late Tuesday night. “But just move on to (Wednesday) and try to put some better at-bats together.”
The challenge of a bullpen game is a hitter rarely sees a pitcher twice and the Padres are especially proficient when they see relievers more than once.
They rank 10th in the majors with a .712 OPS against relievers, but 17th the first time they see a reliever (.704) and first the second time they see a reliever (.998 OPS).
Right-hander Kyle Hurt was the only pitcher to finish two innings and he allowed just one hit and faced seven batters while taking down the sixth and seventh innings.
Left-hander Jack Dreyer and right-hander Edwin Diaz got through their frames without giving up a baserunner. The rest of the slate of relievers all faced five batters or less.
In short, things went about as optimal as the Dodgers could hope for from a unit ranks 12th in the majors with a 3.82 ERA.
“The Dodgers bullpen’s got some good arms in it,” Stammen said. “They’re bringing out guys that have really good stuff. But the best way to do it is to play a little small ball and try to beat them that way. We just didn’t have the opportunity to play that way and score one run at a time (after) we get down 4-0. That kind of eliminates that way of playing baseball. But you know, we’ve seen their arms now for the rest of the series, and hopefully that benefits us going forward the next two days.”
Wednesday’s pitching matchup
Padres LHP Robbie Ray (13-8, 3.60 ERA)
He’s got a 5.22 ERA in eight starts since the trade deadline. His last start (6 IP, 3 ER) was one of three quality starts as a Padre and a 6-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio was his best since the trade. Ray has a 3.81 ERA in 26 career starts against the Dodgers, but he has allowed 15 earned runs in 19 ⅓ runs over four starts over the last two years.
Here is how Ray has fared against current Dodgers:
Dodgers RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-8, 2.51 ERA)
He’s thrown a career-high 179 innings while allowing a career-low 5.7 hits per nine innings. His 14 wins are also a new career best. Yamamoto has a 3.76 ERA in seven regular-season starts against the Padres and a 1.35 ERA in three starts this season (20 (IP, 6 BBs, 22 Ks).
Here is how Yamamoto has fared against current Padres in the regular season:

item.title: [Yahoo] Shohei Ohtani tiene previsto regresar el miércoles, pero los Dodgers aún tienen dudas por resolver
item.dc:creator: Maddie Lee
item.description: A los Dodgers les queda menos de una semana de la temporada regular para ponerse en forma para los playoffs. Y los movimientos en su plantilla para esta serie reflejan esa prisa por el tiempo. El mánager Dave Roberts confirmó el martes que Shohei Ohtani (bíceps derecho, rodilla izquierda) iba a ser reincorporado el miércoles tras su estancia de 15 días en la lista de lesionados. Según Roberts, Ohtani se siente "considerablemente" mejor que antes de estar en la lista de lesionados. "Diría que si
item.content:encoded:
A los Dodgers les queda menos de una semana de la temporada regular para ponerse en forma para los playoffs. Y los movimientos en su plantilla para esta serie reflejan esa prisa por el tiempo.
El mánager Dave Roberts confirmó el martes que Shohei Ohtani (bíceps derecho, rodilla izquierda) iba a ser reincorporado el miércoles tras su estancia de 15 días en la lista de lesionados. Según Roberts, Ohtani se siente "considerablemente" mejor que antes de estar en la lista de lesionados.
"Diría que si antes estaba en un nivel de cinco, ahora probablemente esté en un ocho o un nueve", dijo Roberts antes de que ocho lanzadores lideraran la victoria de los Dodgers por 7-0 contra los Padres de San Diego en el primer partido de la serie.
El martes, los Dodgers redujeron a uno su número mágico para asegurar una exención en la primera ronda. Y antes del partido, recuperaron a otros dos jugadores importantes para la postemporada, al reincorporar del lista de lesionados al jardinero central Andy Pages (fractura en la mano izquierda) y al lanzador derecho Roki Sasaki (ampolla en el dedo medio derecho).
En movimientos correspondientes, los Dodgers enviaron al equipo de Triple A de Oklahoma City al lanzador derecho Emmet Sheehan y al receptor Eliézer Alfonzo.
Sasaki se hizo cargo de la cuarta entrada del partido con relevos y lanzó sin permitir carreras. Permitió un par de sencillos, pero su bola rápida tuvo un poco más de vida en esa breve participación, con un promedio de 98.7 mph y una velocidad máxima de 101.7.
"Pude adaptarme porque ya tenía la experiencia [desde el bullpen] del año pasado", dijo Sasaki a través del intérprete Kensuke Okubo. "Probablemente voy a lanzar en un par de partidos más, así que solo voy a hacer ajustes y seguir avanzando".
Pages se fue de 0 de 2, pero llegó a base dos veces, gracias a un golpeado por lanzamiento y una base por bolas.
"Obviamente, al haber estado fuera un mes, no me siento del todo bien ni tan cómodo al bate", dijo Pages a través del intérprete del equipo, Juan Dorado. "Pero hay cosas [de batear con la máquina Trajekt] que me ayudaron a poder regresar".
Sin embargo, incluso con el regreso de los jugadores, aún hay preguntas que los Dodgers deben responder en la última semana de la temporada:
¿En qué posición bateará Ohtani?
Al menos al principio, Roberts planea colocar a Ohtani al inicio del orden de bateo, como de costumbre. Pero el campocorto Mookie Betts ha entrado en la discusión.
"Sin duda, contra lanzadores diestros [Ohtani] estará ahí", dijo Roberts. "Creo que debería analizar la situación de Mookie contra lanzadores zurdos, pero tengo que pensar en la estructura completa de la alineación".
Ohtani ha sido el primer bateador en todos los partidos que ha sido titular este año. Pero bateó en el segundo lugar en 79 partidos entre las dos temporadas anteriores combinadas.
Incluso sin Ohtani, la alineación de los Dodgers ha estado funcionando bien. El martes, Tommy Edman conectó su segundo jonrón en otros tantos partidos, y Will Smith conectó un jonrón por tercera vez en cuatro días.
¿Está sana la rotación?
El lanzador zurdo de los Dodgers, Blake Snell, quien salió de su apertura la semana pasada por una contractura en la ingle izquierda, realizó una sesión de bullpen el martes. Está programado para una última apertura en la temporada regular el sábado, dijo Roberts.
Eso significa que los cuatro abridores proyectados de los Dodgers para los playoffs están programados para lanzar de este miércoles a sábado, con Yoshinobu Yamamoto y Tyler Glasnow en el montículo para los dos últimos partidos contra los Padres, y Tarik Skubal y Snell en los dos primeros partidos en San Francisco.
¿Quién es el cerrador?
En resumen, podría cambiar de un día para otro.
"En un mundo perfecto —aunque todos sabemos que el mundo no es perfecto—, me encantaría tener [un cerrador fijo]", dijo Roberts. "Creo que si surge la oportunidad, por ejemplo, de que Tanner [Scott] lance una entrada decisiva en la séptima u octava entrada, es difícil dejar pasar esa oportunidad si él es la mejor opción en ese momento. Porque simplemente no sabes cómo se desarrollará la novena entrada.
"Esas son cosas con las que hay que lidiar, y siempre es bueno que la gente las discuta. En este momento no veo a un cerrador que sea solo una persona".
Sasaki asumió ese papel el año pasado. No está claro exactamente cómo lo utilizará Roberts esta vez, pero Roberts dijo que podría ser una opción, dependiendo de cómo lance al regresar de la lista de lesionados.
"El año pasado fue una de esas situaciones de necesidad, dada nuestra situación en cuanto al rendimiento, la salud y la plantilla", dijo Roberts. "Desempeñó ese papel de manera admirable".
El martes, fue uno de los ocho lanzadores de los Dodgers que, en conjunto, lograron una blanqueada en un día de bullpen.
"Hemos tenido mucho talento a lo largo de los años", dijo Roberts. "Pero al sentarnos aquí hoy, al final de la temporada, el bullpen está en la mejor forma en la que ha estado. Eso podría cambiar en un día, en un partido, como todos sabemos. Pero en este momento, me siento muy bien con todos los que están ahí afuera".
El lanzador derecho Edwin Díaz, quien perdió el puesto de cerrador debido a una combinación de lesiones y bajo rendimiento, está en camino de volver a ser considerado para la novena entrada. El martes, retiró a los primeros bateadores de la alineación en orden para una quinta entrada limpia, lo que marcó su tercera salida consecutiva sin permitir carreras desde que regresó de la lista de lesionados.
"Si eres uno de los 12 o 13 lanzadores en una posible lista para la postemporada, estás en la lista de los que gozan de confianza", dijo Roberts. "Y él se ha colocado justo en medio de esa conversación. Y considerando todo lo que ha tenido que pasar este año para enderezar el rumbo, es un gran mérito para él".
¿Quién se queda con el último lugar en la banca?
La contienda por ser el bateador zurdo de la banca en la postemporada se ha reducido al novato Josué De Paula y al receptor lesionado Dalton Rushing (distensión en el flexor derecho). Pero con Rushing aún en la lista de lesionados, De Paula parece tener ventaja.
No le des demasiada importancia al movimiento correspondiente de los Dodgers con respecto a Ohtani el miércoles. Si envían a De Paula a las ligas menores a 10 días del primer partido de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional, aún puede ser incluido en la plantilla.
Los Dodgers tendrán que hacer otro movimiento en la plantilla más adelante en la semana, cuando planean activar a Rushing. Si envían a un jugador a las ligas menores para hacerle espacio a Rushing, ese jugador solo sería elegible para el inicio de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional como transacción correspondiente a un movimiento a la lista de lesionados.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made a massive statement in support of Edwin Diaz, the reliever who has long struggled but has found some form recently.
Edwin Diaz, the closer?
According to Roberts, Diaz has shown enough to be in the conversation for high-leverage relief spots, and possibly even a save opportunity.
“I think it’s one of those things that if you’re one of the 12, 13 pitchers on a potential postseason roster, you’re in the trust tree,” Roberts said.
“And he’s put himself right smack in that conversation. Given all that he’s had to go through this year to right the ship, it’s a big credit to him.”
As for his usage, Roberts could deploy Diaz in a possible save opportunity over his next two relief appearances.
The Dodgers enter Wednesday with five games left, and according to Roberts, Diaz will pitch in two, with one possibly coming in the ninth.
“The way he’s throwing the ninth is possible,” Roberts highlighted.
How has Edwin Diaz pitched recently?
Edwin Diaz returned from the injured list on September 18th against the San Francisco Giants, where he was put into low-leverage spots at first.
He threw a scoreless outing, allowing just one hit and getting two punchouts. Then, he had another scoreless outing the following day, allowing a walk and getting two strikeouts.
Finally, against the San Diego Padres, he got two strikeouts in yet another shutout inning.
In total, he has pitched three innings, with six strikeouts, no runs, one hit, and a walk.
Even more important for Diaz, he has allowed no hard-hit balls or barrels. He has thrown 40 strikes over 60 pitches.
His fastball has life, while his slider has more movement. More importantly, Diaz’s command is better than ever, allowing him to pinpoint pitches and avoid giving up too many walks.
If he keeps this up and his confidence grows, Diaz has the pedigree and experience to be a serious postseason asset, possibly as the closer.

item.title: [mlb.com] The teams no one wants to play in October
item.dc:creator: Travis Sawchik
item.description: The best teams over 162 games and the clubs nobody wants to see in October are not necessarily the same. The regular season and the postseason reward different things. Over six months, baseball is a test of skill and depth. The weakest links eventually get exposed. A team can survive a thin rotation, a shaky middle-relief corps or a few light-hitting positions for a while – but it's much harder to hide those weaknesses over six months. October is different. The games are fewer, off-days greater.
item.content:encoded:
The best teams over 162 games and the clubs nobody wants to see in October are not necessarily the same.
The regular season and the postseason reward different things.
Over six months, baseball is a test of skill and depth. The weakest links eventually get exposed. A team can survive a thin rotation, a shaky middle-relief corps or a few light-hitting positions for a while – but it's much harder to hide those weaknesses over six months.
October is different.
The games are fewer, off-days greater. The urgency is heightened. Teams concentrate work among their best pitchers and lineups. Managers can shorten games with their best relievers. And one superstar hitter or ace can have an outsized influence on a short series.
Variance matters, too. A cleanup hitter can go 2-for-20 in April and the season keeps moving. Go 2-for-20 in October and the season might be over.
“Scary” is not necessarily the same as “best.” It is about concentration of talent, the ability to hide weaknesses, who is peaking at the right time, and the number of ways a team can make a short series tilt quickly.
I started with a simple framework: Which teams can shorten a series with two or three dominant starters? Which have a bullpen capable of essentially ending a game after five or six innings? Which lineups have enough power to avoid having to string together three or four hits against elite pitching? Which teams have deeper lineups to grind down opponents?
Who are the teams nobody wants to see in October?
The concentrated dynamo: the Dodgers
The Dodgers are the obvious answer.
Yes, they have some health question marks with Blake Snell and Shohei Ohtani. Yes, Edwin Díaz has not been the end-game piece they were hoping for in the bullpen. And, yes, their overall team slugging is down double-digit points from each of the last two years as well. But they are still a heavy World Series favorite no one wants to play.
A rotation led by Snell, Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow is as good as it gets, and they are backed by a lineup that, while aging, still ranks as one of the best in the game. The market and models still believe they are the team to beat; FanGraphs gives them a 29.3% chance to win the title.
The team without a weakness: Brewers
While the Dodgers are the favorites, there's a case to be made that the Brewers are the scarier October opponent.
And after struggling out of the gate, Milwaukee is 82-44 since May 1 – five games better than the Rays, the next-ranking team. They've been above average in every month since April.
The terrifying thing about the Brewers is that there isn't an obvious way to attack them.
They have the most dominant pitcher in the game this year in Jacob Misiorowski, who unlike in his rookie year has shown no signs of slowing down. Misiorowski remains dominant in the second half with a 29% K-BB mark. His elevated velocity has held steady. And nearly as unhittable in the second half is Logan Henderson, who sports a 2.22 ERA, is holding opponents to a .171 average, and enjoys a 26.9 K-BB% mark since the All-Star break.
Getting the starter out doesn't make life easier either. The Brewers' reliever corps ranks fourth in ERA (3.41) and third in fWAR (6.6) out of all 30 teams.
Supporting those arms is an excellent defense.
And while the Brewers lack elite power, they string together quality at-bats with seven qualified Brewers hitters having an OPS+ of 100 or better, trailing only the Dodgers (eight) in the projected postseason field. The Phillies, by contrast, have two.
They are also trending the right way. The Brewers are 17-9 over the 30 days, tied for the second-best mark in baseball.
FanGraphs gives the Brewers the second-best title chances after the Dodgers (13.9%). They are a team built for the regular season and October.
OK, those are obvious contenders. What about other clubs?
The middling (potential) division winner: Guardians
The Guardians were one of the teams that actually won the Trade Deadline. Those added reinforcements, along with some positive regression from first-half slumpers like Steven Kwan, picked up a sluggish offense. They rank eighth in the Majors in runs since Aug. 1 (216 entering Tuesday).
A less obvious October advantage? Cleveland leads baseball in the percentage of plate appearances in which it enjoys the platoon advantage, at 77%, compared with a league average of 58.3%. In a five-game or seven-game series against a manager trying to optimize every matchup, that can become consequential.
And what really makes this team dangerous is the pitching staff.
The Guardians are one of three teams projected to be in the field that roster two pitchers that rank in the top 10 of fWAR in the second half of the season (the Dodgers are another, along with the Phillies).
Gavin Williams and Parker Messick have emerged as front-line starters this year. Tanner Bibee is a strong No. 3. While middle relief has hurt the club all season, being able to move a starter to the relief group should build a better bridge to closer Cade Smith.
Most teams that spend much of a season hovering around .500 don't have this kind of top-end pitching.
The Guardians are also hot, tied for the second-best record (17-9) in the Majors over the last month – tied with the Dodgers, Brewers, Braves and Padres – entering play Tuesday. Only the Rays (19-8) are better – but the Rays don't quite have the Guardians’ top-end starting pitching depth.
As the playoff picture stands entering Tuesday, the Guardians would face the winner of the White Sox (+42 run differential) or Rangers (-34 run differential) in the ALDS, with AL East clubs competing on the other side of the bracket. That's an extremely favorable path for a team with sneaky upside.
The unusual build: Cubs 
The Cubs are perhaps the strangest team on this list because their postseason case is built around the idea that an elite lineup and defense can overwhelm the quality and concentration of October pitching.
In the second half they've posted a 125 wRC+, 25% better than league average, and they've combined for a 134 wRC+ over the last month. That's an incredible number.
The 2018 Dodgers are an interesting comp. They led the NL with a 111 wRC+, including a 134 mark over the last 30 days of the season – just like these surging Cubs. They were also an elite defensive team lacking an elite rotation.
Those Dodgers won a relatively modest 92 games in the regular season but advanced to the World Series. Perhaps the Cubs can, too. While an ace makes life easier, there are different paths through October.
The wild card among wild cards: Padres
If you believe in timing and momentum, believe in the Padres.
For much of the season they have been a confounding team, much like their face of the franchise, Fernando Tatis Jr.
Over the last month, the Padres are third in baseball with a 118 wRC+.
Moreover, the pitching has become more interesting – deeper and healthier – at exactly the right time.
Nick Pivetta returned from his long absence to post a 1.93 ERA over three September starts.
Michael King has outperformed peripherals to become a 12-game winner with a 3.03 ERA. Robbie Ray, acquired at the Trade Deadline, gives them another veteran option.
They also have one great postseason advantage: If they can hand a lead over to the bullpen it's lights out with Adrian Morejon and Mason Miller closing out games.
The Padres own the end game, and at no time does that matter more than in October.

item.title: [True Blue LA] Sidelined last year, Evan Phillips & Brock Stewart are ready for October
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Last year at this time, Evan Phillips and Brock Stewart were both recovering from surgeries and unavailable to pitch. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Last year at this time, Evan Phillips and Brock Stewart were both recovering from surgeries and unavailable to pitch. They were around the team but unable to contribute during the stretch run and postseason. This year, both veteran right-handers are two key cogs in an increasingly deep Dodgers bullpen and an important part of their October puzzle.
Phillips had Tommy John surgery in June 2025, wiping out the last half of last season and the first half of this one. When he returned from the injured list in July, the Dodgers were cautious in his usage, not using him on back-to-back days for his first four weeks, and used him on one day rest only four times during that stretch.
The results were spotty at first, allowing runs in five of his first seven appearances, including an uncharacteristic four home runs in such a short span. Since then, Phillips has allowed runs in only three of his last 21 appearances, and the lone home run surrendered was last Monday to Elly De La Cruz, which seems to be a rite of passage for everybody these days.
“Evan as you would expect, the first handful of outings were inconsistent coming off Tommy John, but I’d say the last [few] have been kind of who he is, and it’s been fun to see,” manager Dave Roberts said recently. “There’s a two-seamer, there’s a four-seamer, and some sweepers getting some awkward swings, some chase. That’s been good, and his command has been a lot better, too.”
Phillips in his 28 games has 28 strikeouts against only three unintentional walks. Since the start of August, the Dodgers have used Phillips more aggressively, pitching on back-to-back days five times, and he pitched three times in four days in three different stretches, and during that span has a 2.30 ERA and 2.46 FIP.
“I appreciate what they’ve done, trying to build me up, plus also protect me, plus giving me advantageous lanes while also challenging me,” Phillips said. “It’s been great so far, and I definitely feel like I’m coming closer and closer to that best version of myself that I have been and continue to strive to be.”
Stewart, a sixth-round draft pick of the Dodgers in 2014, was reacquired by the team at the 2025 trade deadline, but he pitched in only four games for them before succumbing to right shoulder debridement surgery in September. This year the right-hander has a 2.45 ERA and 2.53 xERA in his 27 games, with 24 strikeouts and seven unintentional walks in 25 2/3 innings, including a scoreless first inning to start Tuesday night’s bullpen-game shutout of the San Diego Padres.
“When Brock’s healthy, he’s as good as anyone we have,” Roberts said Tuesday. “For us, it’s just trying to manage him the right way and keep him strong and healthy. He’s been great.”
“That’s very cool to hear. I just go out there and throw it, that’s literally all I focus on. But people tell me that my — you know, I throw five pitches, which helps as a reliever,” Stewart said. “They tell me my stuff is pretty good, and it’s always nice to hear that. But I don’t know, I just go out there and throw it, try to compete as best I can, and hope it works out.
Roberts wasn’t wrong. Since returning to the majors in 2023 with the Minnesota Twins, Stewart has a 2.45 ERA and 2.78 xERA, which ranks 10th and ninth, respectively, among the 576 major league pitchers with at least 100 innings over the last four years. Tarik Skubal, with two Cy Young Awards during that stretch, has a 2.50 ERA and 2.73 xERA, for example.
But staying on the field has been a problem for Stewart, who this season alone has been on the injured list three different times — recovering from shoulder surgery, bone spur in his left foot, and shoulder discomfort — inactive for a total of 95 games. Since 2023, Stewart has also been on the injured list with elbow soreness, shoulder tendinitis, a shoulder strain, a hamstring strain, and shoulder inflammation, limited to just 106 2/3 total innings over the last four seasons.
“I feel good, but I’ve told everybody though, one day at a time. I’ve been hurt a lot so I always try to take things one day at a time. But I’m happy with the way I feel, happy with the way I felt today,” Stewart said. “Getting close to the finish line, but happy with how I feel, happy with how the stuff is coming out. I feel like I’m in a good spot and can hopefully help out.”
Stewart has pitched in the postseason only once, in three games over two series with the Minnesota Twins in 2023. Phillips was an October stalwart for the Dodgers since he was acquired on a waiver claim in 2021. In 12 appearances for the Dodgers in the playoffs, Phillips has yet to allow a run, over 15 1/3 innings, with 21 strikeouts and six unintentional walks. Phillips missed out on the World Series in 2024 with a right rotator cuff injury suffered during the NLCS, and was sidelined for all of last October.
“I love pitching in the postseason, I love competing with these guys. In 2024, missing out on the World Series, but I tried to dig in on the fact that I helped us get there, and played quite a large part in the Division Series and Championship Series. Obviously I want to see it all to the end, and help us carry that trophy off the field,” Philips said. “I’m just as eager as ever. Fortunate that I feel healthy at this time, and just trying to build on that, continue to chip away, and be the best I can when it matters most.”
This season, only Tanner Scott, Edwin Díaz, and Alex Vesia have a higher average-leverage index than Phillips and Stewart among Dodgers relievers. Phillips and Stewart have each saved a game this year, and Phillips has done so in the past with 46 saves with the Dodgers. Roberts said he’d feel comfortable with either Phillips or Stewart getting a save opportunity in October, along with a group that includes Tanner Scott and the just-activated Roki Sasaki.
“This year, more than any other year, I think there’s more guys we feel comfortable closing out games,” Roberts said.

item.title: [New York Post] Roki Sasaki ditches Dodgers plan with striking U-turn in prep for 3-peat quest
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: The initial plan called for Roki Sasaki to pitch an inning or two as an opener. Sasaki had other ideas. “I said I wanted to pitch out of the bullpen,” Sasaki said in Japanese. Because Sasaki will be deployed as a reliever in the playoffs, he figured he should spend the remainder of the regular season becoming reacquainted with the role. So instead of throwing the first and second innings of the Dodgers’ 7-0 victory over the San Diego Padres on Tuesday night, Sasaki pitched the fourth. Returning
item.content:encoded:
The initial plan called for Roki Sasaki to pitch an inning or two as an opener.
Sasaki had other ideas.
“I said I wanted to pitch out of the bullpen,” Sasaki said in Japanese.
Because Sasaki will be deployed as a reliever in the playoffs, he figured he should spend the remainder of the regular season becoming reacquainted with the role.
So instead of throwing the first and second innings of the Dodgers’ 7-0 victory over the San Diego Padres on Tuesday night, Sasaki pitched the fourth.
Returning from a month-long stay on the injured list, Sasaki pitched in relief for the first time this season.
What was most memorable about his night wasn’t that he struck out two batters or threw six of his 20 pitches faster than 99 mph. Rather, what was most striking was his embrace of his move out of the Dodgers’ rotation.
Sasaki was reluctant to make the switch last year, doing so only as a last-ditch effort to salvage an otherwise disastrous rookie season. The decision made him an October hero, as the team’s lack of options made him the closer almost by default.
He returned to the rotation this year and was 5-5 with a 4.56 earned-run average through his first 23 games, all of them starts. His form improved over the course of the season, and he was 2-0 with a 3.05 ERA in seven starts after the All-Star break. But in the last of those starts, which was on Aug. 26 in Atlanta, he developed a blister on the middle finger of his pitching hand.
Starting games was a source of pride for Sasaki. When he agreed to try pitching in relief last year, he made the Dodgers promise him they would use him as a starter this season.
Sasaki didn’t require as much convincing when team officials started talking to him about a role change on the Dodgers’ recent trip to Cincinnati.
The Dodgers will use a four-man rotation in the playoffs, and they have four Cy Young Award-caliber pitchers in Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow. Sasaki could do the math. If he was going to pitch in the postseason, it would be as a reliever.
“I think it’s important to make the roster,” Sasaki said.
Something else: The Dodgers kept their word about him starting games, and Sasaki wanted to repay them.
“In the first half of the season, they used me as a starter even when I wasn’t pitching well,” he said.
Sasaki didn’t pitch more than five innings in any of his first five starts. His ERA at that point was 6.35. His fastball velocity was down and his command was non-existent.
The Dodgers would have been justified in removing him from the rotation.
They didn’t.
They could have sent him to the minor leagues.
They didn’t.
That meant something to Sasaki.
“This time,” Sasaki said, “I want to be able to contribute to the team in whatever shape.”
The feelings point to a growing trust that has developed between Sasaki and the Dodgers.
At this stage of the season last year, they didn’t seem to be on the same page. As he shined as their closer last October, Dodgers officials and coaches told stories about how they helped Sasaki rediscover his 100-mph fastball. Sasaki downplayed the team’s role in his resurgence, saying he figured out what he was doing wrong by watching videos of himself pitching in high school.
Sasaki is said to have become more open to instruction this season, which contributed to an improved fastball as well as the incorporation of a different variation of his signature forkball.
He is also physically stronger than he did last year. Fatigue was a factor for him in the postseason, and by the World Series, he looked like a spent cartridge. To close out Game 7 of the World Series, manager Dave Roberts went to Yamamoto, who was pitching his third inning in relief a day after making a six-inning start.
Sasaki looks more capable of shouldering a reliever’s schedule and workload.
Sasaki closing games in the upcoming postseason is “certainly an option,” manager Dave Roberts said.
Edwin Diaz has worked his way back into ninth-inning consideration by posting three consecutive scoreless appearances since his return from his latest IL stint. Tanner Scott has been the Dodgers’ primary closer this season, but Roberts said there could be instances in which the left-hander is used earlier in games in high-leverage situations.
Sasaki said he would pitch whenever asked.
That could be determined by how he looks over this final week of the regular season. Roberts said he will likely pitch next on Friday in San Francisco.
This time around, there isn’t any hesitation on the part of Sasaki. This time around, he really wants to do this.

item.title: [Just Baseball] The Dodgers' Max Muncy Continues To Be Underrated | Just Baseball
item.dc:creator: Clay Snowden
item.description: Los Angeles, California. The city of movie stars, names and big personalities. Oh yeah, and championships, with the two most recent going to the Dodgers. item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles, California. The city of movie stars, names and big personalities. Oh yeah, and championships, with the two most recent going to the Dodgers. When you think about the Los Angeles Dodgers, the names that come to mind are Shohei, Tarik, Yoshinobu, and Mookie.
Not Max.
For one reason or another, Max Muncy has been an underappreciated player in this league for far too long. No, he’s not the typical profile to win an MVP; he doesn’t have the flair that matches the city, and maybe consistency just isn’t sexy.
But, remove Max Muncy from the Los Angeles Dodgers, and this season, along with their recent history, looks different.
Stats from prior to games on Sept. 20, 2026.
Muncy’s Importance in 2026
Although the Dodgers easily clinched another NL West title, I think it’s fair to say their season has not gone quite as planned. Crazy, right? When you have their amount of star power and top prospects, and you acquire Tarik Skubal at the deadline, anything less than the best record in baseball isn’t good enough.
Part of the reason why the Dodgers have not reached the extremely high expectations many placed on them is injuries. Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith, Roki Sasaki, Andy Pages, Dalton Rushing, Edwin Díaz, Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, and others all missed significant time on the IL.
Combine that IL time with Kyle Tucker’s ho-hum season and Mookie Betts not being quite the player he once was at the plate, and you can see why the Dodgers don’t quite look like an unstoppable force.
With so many injuries and inconsistencies in the lineup, the Dodgers needed Max Muncy more than ever. Even at 36 years old, Muncy is having an amazing season. He is slashing .254/.351/.500 with 29 home runs and a 132 wRC+, second on the team only to Ohtani’s 142 wRC+. Muncy’s 4.3 fWAR is first amongst Dodgers position players. Yes, that includes Ohtani.
He’s currently on pace to either match or surpass his career high of 4.5 fWAR from the 2021 season when he hit 36 home runs. If he doesn’t quite get to 4.5, 4.4 would tie his second-best season, which came in 2019 in the juiced-ball era. Yeah, I’d say Muncy’s doing pretty well.
After being such a consistent and healthy player throughout the beginning part of his career, Muncy missed parts of the last two seasons due to injury. Returning from injury to play over 140 games, and at this high of a level, goes to show what type of talent he is.
On the current roster, Muncy is one of three players with more than 20 home runs. Keep in mind, Ohtani also has more than 20, but he is on the IL. Muncy’s 29 home runs place him in the top 20 in all of baseball. We still saw his power in his injury-riddled seasons in 2024 and 2025, but seeing it return to this level has been a massive boost for the Dodgers.
Kyle Tucker was seen as a middle-of-the-order bat who could push Muncy down a spot, but as it has turned out, Muncy is more important than ever. Sure, this team would still have topped 90 wins without Muncy, but the lineup would feel much different. The hole created at third base would be filled by Miguel Rojas or Enrique Hernández, which is far from ideal. The drop-off from Muncy to whoever the replacement was would have been massive.
As you look ahead to the postseason, there are still questions around the Dodgers’ lineup. Pages recently returned from the IL, and Ohtani will soon, giving the Dodgers a much-needed boost. Pages adds another righty bat into the lineup and allows Tommy Edman to move back to the infield. Ohtani fills DH, which is currently held down by rookie Josue De Paula.
Muncy adds another veteran back with postseason experience. A .817 OPS and 16 career postseason home runs give the Dodgers another threat once the weather cools and the games become more important.
Yes, Muncy has been crucial to the Dodgers’ success this season. But you could really say that about his entire career.
Muncy’s Consistent Excellence
Let’s start back at the beginning. Max Muncy started with the Oakland Athletics before being released in 2017 and signing a minor league contract with the Dodgers. He debuted in LA in 2018, immediately finding success, slashing .263/.391/.582 with 35 home runs. From an Oakland castoff to hitting 35 home runs a year later was impressive, but it was just the beginning.
Muncy followed in 2019, repeating his 35-home run season, a mark he has posted four times since joining the Dodgers. Power has been an important part of his game, and so has consistency. From 2018 through 2023, Muncy logged at least 135 games each year, excluding the COVID season.
Of those six seasons, three were at 130 wRC+ or better, and five were over 100. Really, the only subpar season of his career came in 2020, when he had a 98 wRC+ and 12 home runs in 58 games.
His 2024 and 2025 shortened seasons were still, statistically, some of the best of his career. If we look at it just from a wRC+ standpoint, his 133 wRC+ in 2024 and 137 in 2025 rank in the top four in his career, while 2026 (132 wRC+) lands in the same discussion.
By now, you know what you’re getting with Muncy. Consistent power and one of the best walk rates in the league. His batting average isn’t going to wow anyone, and neither is his defense, although both are adequate in this day and age.
Max Muncy is one of the best Dodgers of all time, and you might not even realize it. His 238 career home runs rank fifth in Dodger history. He ranks seventh in walks, roughly 100 behind Jackie Robinson. Only 14 Dodgers have driven in more runs, and by the time Muncy hangs up the cleats, he could be near the top 10.
Year in and year out, Muncy gives the Dodgers exactly what they expect of him. Early in his career, he provided versatility around the diamond. If the team needed a second baseman, he’d play there. When they needed a first baseman in 2021, Muncy was the answer. Now, he’s settled into third base.
Three All-Star appearances and three World Series rings. I’d argue that he deserves more recognition. Not too bad for a guy that they got for next to nothing.
Final Thoughts
I know that the Dodgers have the type of star power that drives jersey sales. Who wouldn’t want to wear an Ohtani jersey? He’s the best player to ever play the game.
However, I wish we would see more Muncy jerseys at Dodger Stadium. In some ways, this might be a “you don’t know what you’ve got till it’s gone” situation. Luckily, I think Muncy still has several more productive seasons left. He’s not showing signs of slowing down.
If you placed Max Muncy into a number of other cities, he would be their star. I guess it’s easy to get lost in Hollywood, which has over 2,800 of them.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers leave door open to Edwin Diaz reclaiming closer’s role: ‘Certainly possible’
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: In a perfect world, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said, the team would like to have one set closer entering the playoffs. And by the end of Tuesday’s 7-0 win over the San Diego Padres, one unexpected name might have thrown their hat back into the ring. A week ago, the Dodgers were not certain Edwin Díaz would even be on their playoff roster, after the $69 million offseason signing lost his closer job amid an injury-plagued season marred by an ERA of nearly 12.00. In three outings since returning
item.content:encoded:
In a perfect world, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said, the team would like to have one set closer entering the playoffs.
And by the end of Tuesday’s 7-0 win over the San Diego Padres, one unexpected name might have thrown their hat back into the ring.
A week ago, the Dodgers were not certain Edwin Díaz would even be on their playoff roster, after the $69 million offseason signing lost his closer job amid an injury-plagued season marred by an ERA of nearly 12.00.
In three outings since returning from the injured list, however, the three-time All-Star has suddenly looked like his old dominant self again.
So much so, Roberts said it remains “certainly possible” that he could factor into the Dodgers’ ninth-inning October plans.
Roberts made that claim after Díaz’s best performance yet, when he retired the top of the Padres’ batting order in order in a dominant fifth-inning sequence.
That marked the right-hander’s third scoreless appearance in a row –– a stretch that has included only one hit, one walk and six strikeouts –– and continued an unforeseen return to form triggered by a recent mechanical adjustment he made during a minor-league rehab stint.
“His last three have been fantastic with us,” Roberts said. “I wanted to see him against their better hitters, and he did a really nice job.”
Indeed, Díaz began his inning by ringing up Fernando Tatis Jr. on a front-door slider. He then fanned Dustin Harris at the end of a nine-pitch at-bat with a swing-and-miss slider. Had he used an ABS challenge, he could have punched out Manny Machado too. But he retired him all the same with a soft tapper back to the mound.
“Given all that he’s had to go through this year,” Roberts said, “to right the ship is a big credit to him.”
But will it be enough to put him back in consideration for closing duties?
Roberts made sure not to shut that door yet.
“The way he’s throwing, the ninth is possible, yes,” the manager said.
At the very least, it adds one more subplot to the final week of the Dodgers’ regular season.
The team, of course, has other closer options to consider. Tanner Scott has converted 23 of 27 save opportunities with a 2.77 ERA as Díaz’s replacement this year. Roki Sasaki has also returned to relief duties as he did at the end of last season, when he emerged as an emergency closing option during the Dodgers’ run to a second-straight World Series.
And as Roberts noted Tuesday, a closer-by-committee plan remains in play, as well.
But as the Dodgers set out for a three-peat this year, they always envisioned Díaz –– and his trademark trumpet bullpen entrance –– being a staple at the end of games.
Though he suffered a career-worst campaign, converting just seven of 11 save opportunities while missing three months with an elbow injury and another with neck inflammation, there might be time for him to reclaim his original role yet.

item.title: [ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos] Dodgers score 5 two-out runs off Padres starter Michael King in 7-0 victory

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers score 5 two-out runs off Padres starter Michael King in 7-0 victory
Tommy Edman and Will Smith homered as the Los Angeles Dodgers scored six runs with two outs to beat the San Diego Padres 7-0 in a series opener between rivals with the two best records in the majors this month
LOS ANGELES -- Tommy Edman and Will Smith homered as the Los Angeles Dodgers scored six runs with two outs to beat the San Diego Padres 7-0 on Tuesday night in a series opener between rivals with the two best records in the majors this month.
The Dodgers (97-60) moved within one game of NL Central champion Milwaukee (98-59) for the top mark in the big leagues and home-field advantage throughout the postseason. However, the Brewers own the head-to-head tiebreaker.
Los Angeles needs one win or an Atlanta loss to clinch a first-round bye into a National League Division Series.
The NL West champion Dodgers improved to 15-5 in September with their fifth straight victory; the Padres fell to 14-5 and had their five-game winning streak snapped.
San Diego is tied with Chicago and Philadelphia at 87-70 for the three NL wild cards — four games ahead of Arizona with five to play.
Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado were a combined 1 for 7 with five strikeouts for the Padres.
The Dodgers chased Michael King (12-10) after four innings in his career-high 32nd start of the season. The right-hander gave up five runs on six hits and struck out five as his four-game winning streak ended.
Los Angeles broke out with four runs in the second. King got the first two outs on six pitches before loading the bases. Teoscar Hernández and rookie Josue De Paula hit consecutive singles before King plunked Andy Pages, who just came off the injured list.
King then issued back-to-back walks to Edman and Mookie Betts, forcing in two runs. Freddie Freeman's two-run single made it 4-0.
Betts had a ground-rule double and scored on Freeman's two-out single for a 5-0 lead in the fourth.
Edman's solo shot came with two outs in the sixth and Smith added a 396-foot drive with one out in the seventh for a 7-0 lead.
Brock Stewart started a bullpen game and Justin Wrobleski (12-5) got the win for the Dodgers, who used eight pitchers to earn the fifth shutout in franchise history when deploying at least that many.
Among them was reliever Edwin Díaz, who struck out two in one inning. Roki Sasaki's four-seam fastball touched 100 mph while he pitched one inning. The Japanese right-hander came off the injured list earlier Tuesday after missing nearly a month with a blister on his right middle finger.
Padres LHP Robbie Ray (13-8, 3.60 ERA) starts Wednesday against Dodgers RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-8, 2.51).
___
This story has been corrected to show the Dodgers scored six runs with two outs, not five.
___

item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen

item.content:encoded:
LOS ÁNGELES -- Roki Sasaki llamó la atención cuando pasó al bullpen durante la marcha del año pasado hacia el bicampeonato. Volverá a desempeñar ese papel en los últimos días de esta temporada regular y posiblemente vuelva a estar entre las opciones para cerrar juegos.
Sasaki fue activado de la lista de lesionados de 15 días antes de la victoria por 7-0 sobre los Padres la noche del martes, como parte de una serie de movimientos que también incluyeron el regreso del cubano Andy Pagés de la lista de lesionados y el envío de Emmet Sheehan y el venezolano Eliezer Alfonzo a Triple-A Oklahoma City. Sasaki lanzó por última vez el 26 de agosto, cuando una ampolla en el dedo medio de la mano derecha puso fin prematuramente a su apertura contra los Bravos.
En su segunda temporada en Grandes Ligas, Sasaki se acercaba cada vez más a la versión de sí mismo que fue un fenómeno en la Liga Japonesa de Béisbol Profesional (NPB, por sus siglas en inglés). Tuvo marca de 5-5 con efectividad de 4.60 en 23 aperturas, pero esos números no cuentan toda la historia. Con un repertorio más amplio, que incluye un nuevo splitter, y una mayor velocidad en su recta, Sasaki tuvo su mejor tramo sostenido como abridor en Grandes Ligas, registrando efectividad de 2.63 en siete aperturas antes de lidiar con la ampolla.
“Emocionado de tener a Roki de vuelta”, dijo el manager Dave Roberts. “Está entusiasmado con este rol. Creo que puede tener un gran impacto, como lo tuvo el año pasado”.
En su regreso al bullpen el martes, Sasaki ponchó a dos en un cuarto inning en blanco, pese a permitir un par de sencillos con dos outs. Generó cuatro swings fallidos, incluidos dos en igual número de swings contra su splitter, y promedió 98.7 mph con las ocho rectas que lanzó, ligeramente por encima de su promedio de 97.8 mph esta temporada.
Los Dodgers mejoraron su récord a 97-60 después de que su juego de bullpen terminara en blanqueada. Están cinco juegos por delante de los Bravos en la lucha por el segundo mejor récord de la Liga Nacional y a uno de los Cerveceros, líderes del circuito y dueños del criterio de desempate entre ambos.
El año pasado, el traslado de Sasaki al relevo fue una decisión sin precedentes. Después de un comienzo por debajo de las expectativas en su temporada de novato y de perderse más de cuatro meses por una lesión en el hombro, la única oportunidad de Sasaki de contribuir con los Dodgers en la postemporada era pasar al bullpen.
Sasaki no sólo contribuyó, sino que se convirtió en el cerrador de los Dodgers en la postemporada, permitiendo apenas una carrera limpia en 10.2 innings, para efectividad de 0.84. La confianza que adquirió al conseguir resultados en Grandes Ligas, bajo la máxima presión, impulsó el regreso del derecho de 24 años a la rotación y su posterior despegue a mitad de esta temporada.
Actualmente, los Dodgers no cuentan con un cerrador fijo, ya que el boricua Edwin Díaz está lanzando en situaciones de baja presión en medio de sus dificultades a lo largo de la temporada, mientras busca ganarse un puesto en el bullpen para la postemporada. Díaz ponchó a dos en un quinto inning perfecto la noche del martes, su tercera presentación sin permitir carreras desde que regresó de la lista de lesionados.
Ha pasado mucho tiempo desde que Sasaki lanzó como relevista, pero si logra mostrarle lo suficiente a Roberts durante la última semana antes de la postemporada, podría convertirse en una opción para situaciones de salvamento.
“Creo que sin duda es una opción”, dijo Roberts. “Probablemente mucho dependerá de cómo lance esta noche. Seguramente tendrá una o dos presentaciones cortas más antes de que termine la temporada”.
Con Díaz perdiendo tiempo de juego por lesiones en el codo y el cuello, además de no lanzar bien cuando estuvo saludable, el zurdo Tanner Scott ha recibido la mayoría de las oportunidades de salvamento. Scott lidera a los Dodgers con 23 rescates, pero también ha desperdiciado cuatro oportunidades, incluidas dos desde comienzos de septiembre.
Scott todavía podría ser la mejor opción para cerrar los juegos, pero Sasaki podría complementarlo desde el lado derecho, algo importante debido a que el derecho venezolano Edgardo Henríquez estará fuera por el resto de la temporada regular debido a una distensión en la parte baja de la espalda. Se espera que regrese durante la postemporada.
Aunque a Roberts le gustaría contar con un cerrador en la postemporada, reconoció que es más probable que maneje el bullpen según los enfrentamientos. En esta época del año, algunas de las situaciones de mayor presión se presentan antes del noveno inning, por lo que tener varias opciones le permitiría utilizar a sus mejores relevistas en los momentos más convenientes.
“Creo que si hay una oportunidad, por ejemplo, de que Tanner lance un inning de alta presión en el séptimo u octavo, es difícil dejarla pasar si es la mejor opción en ese momento”, dijo Roberts. “Porque simplemente no sabes cómo se va a presentar el noveno inning”.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers shutout of Padres reveals potential (and unexpected) playoff strength
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris

item.content:encoded:
Last year, the Dodgers hardly used their bullpen in the playoffs.
This year, they would like that to once again be the blueprint.
In their bid to three-peat as World Series champions, of course, the Dodgers are expected to be led by their star-studded rotation. Shohei Ohtani isn’t pitching, but Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow are.
And if all goes according to plan, they will handle the bulk of the innings.
However, replicating the starting pitching excellence of last October won’t be easy. A season ago, the Dodgers’ four-man rotation of Ohtani, Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow accounted for 113 of the team’s 165 postseason innings (including relief appearances from Glasnow and Yamamoto). Together, they posted a 2.55 ERA.
It was historic production.
Which also means, it’s fair to assume some regression will be possible –– both in workload and effectiveness.
Thus, having more reliable bullpen options this time around could be equally important for the Dodgers. And while that might have felt like a daunting reality earlier this year, when the unit was banged up and struggling through the middle portion of the campaign, Tuesday night was a reminder that the relief corps could be a strength in this fall’s title pursuit.
“Obviously we’ve had a lot of talent over the years,” manager Dave Roberts said. “But as far as sitting here today at the end of the season, it’s as good of shape as we’ve ever been in with the bullpen.”
In a 7-0 win over the San Diego Padres, the Dodgers were not supposed to have the pitching matchup –– countering Padres ace Michael King with a makeshift bullpen game in a rivalry series opener at Dodger Stadium.
Instead, eight different Dodgers relievers held the previous red-hot Padres to a five-hit shutout. Along the way, several arms who once seemed like question marks continued to round into increasingly promising form.
“It was fantastic,” Roberts said. “This is as good as our bullpen has been, has thrown.”
It started with opener Brock Stewart, a key right-handed weapon in the Dodgers’ bullpen who began the game with a scoreless first inning, continuing his late-season resurgence after another injury-plagued year.
From there, the baton was passed on down.
Justin Wrobleski, who is in the midst of a late-season conversion to the bullpen for the second-straight year, escaped a jam in the second. Blake Treinen, who might be on the postseason roster bubble given the Dodgers’ relief depth, offered one of his best outings of late by issuing only a two-out walk in a scoreless third.

The highlight of the night came in the fourth and fifth, when Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz hung a couple more zeroes in what were important appearances from each.
For Sasaki, the outing marked his first since returning from the injured list and making his own late-season move back to the bullpen, where he could reprise his role as closer from last year’s playoffs. He worked around a pair of singles with two strikeouts and a fastball that, even after being sidelined for the last month by a blister, sat at 99-100 mph.
For Díaz, Tuesday was not only a third-consecutive scoreless outing since his own return from the IL, but his most impressive yet as he makes a bid for the playoff roster. He retired the top of the Padres lineup in order with a pair of strikeouts, and has now retired 9 of 11 batters he has faced since rejoining the active roster.
Asked postgame if Díaz –– the $69 million offseason signing who lost the closer’s job amid a previously dismal debut Dodgers season –– could still pitch his way back into ninth-inning duties, Roberts said it’s “certainly possible.”
“The way he’s throwing, the ninth is possible, yes,” Roberts added.
By that point, the Dodgers had already pulled away from the Padres. They mounted a four-run rally with two outs in the second against King, who issued back-to-back bases-loaded walks to Tommy Edman and Mookie Betts before Freddie Freeman slashed a two-run single through the infield. The offense tacked on more runs in the fourth (on another Freeman RBI single), the sixth (on a solo home run from Tommy Edman), and the seventh (a Will Smith solo blast).
In what was the lineup’s toughest test in a while, they passed with flying colors.
Still, the night’s most encouraging developments came from the ‘pen, which capped off the game with two scoreless innings from Kyle Hurt, then stress-free appearances in the eighth and ninth from Alex Vesia and Jack Dreyer.
The unit’s most trusted arms at the moment, Tanner Scott (who figures to be vying with Sasaki for the postseason closer role) and Evan Phillips, weren’t even required. Nor was Edgardo Henriquez, who remains sidelined by a back injury but still could return in time for the playoffs.
“We know we have a good group, and anytime we get to carry the load and everybody has success and throws up zeros, it’s special,” Stewart said. “That’s really hard to do, for all eight guys or whatever it was today. So yeah, it’s cool.”
With a smirk, he added: “Write stories about it.”
Come October, of course, the Dodgers will be hoping their relievers are the main story.
But if the rotation falters, the club seems significantly better-suited to handle it than it did a year ago.
“That could change in a day, in a game, as we all know,” Roberts said. “But right now, feel really good about everyone out there.”

item.title: [MLB.com] Sasaki returns in relief role as Dodgers assess bullpen options for postseason
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Roki Sasaki opened eyes when he moved to the bullpen for last year's run to back-to-back championships. He'll reprise that role in the final days of this regular season -- and possibly be in the mix to close out games once again.
Sasaki was activated from the 15-day injured list ahead of Tuesday night's series opener against the Padres amid a flurry of moves that also saw Andy Pages return from the IL and Emmet Sheehan and Eliezer Alfonzo get optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City. Sasaki last pitched on Aug. 26, when a blister on his right middle finger brought his start against the Braves to a premature end.
In his second Major League season, Sasaki was steadily growing closer to resembling the version of himself who was a phenom in Nippon Professional Baseball. He went 5-5 with a 4.60 ERA through 23 starts, but those numbers don't tell the full story. Working with an expanded pitch mix, including a new splitter, and increased fastball velocity, Sasaki put together his best sustained stretch as an MLB starter, recording a 2.63 ERA through seven starts before dealing with the blister.
"Excited to see Roki back," manager Dave Roberts said. "He's looking forward to this role. I think he can be very impactful, as it was last year."
In his return to the bullpen on Tuesday, Sasaki was available to pitch multiple innings. He will likely get a couple of additional relief appearances in the final five games of the regular season.
Last year, Sasaki's shift to relief was an unprecedented move. After underperforming to begin his rookie season and then missing more than four months with a shoulder injury, Sasaki's only chance to contribute to the Dodgers in the postseason was to move to the 'pen.
Sasaki didn't just contribute -- he became the Dodgers' postseason closer, allowing just one earned run in 10 2/3 innings (0.84 ERA). The confidence he gained from getting results at the big league level, with the stakes as high as could be, fueled the 24-year-old right-hander's return to the rotation and eventual midseason breakout this year.
The Dodgers are currently working without a set closer, as Edwin Díaz is pitching in low leverage amid his season-long struggles as he looks to earn a role in the postseason bullpen. It has been a long time since Sasaki has pitched in relief, but if he can show Roberts enough in the final week before the postseason, he could very well be an option in save situations.
"I think it's certainly an option," Roberts said. "A lot of it, probably, is contingent on how he throws here tonight. He'll probably get another one or two shorter stints before the season's end."
With Díaz missing time with elbow and neck injuries -- and not pitching well when healthy -- left-hander Tanner Scott has gotten the bulk of save opportunities. Scott leads the Dodgers with 23 saves, but he's also blown four saves, including two since the start of September.
Scott may still be the best option to close out games, but Sasaki could complement him from the right-hand side, which is important with leverage righty Edgardo Henriquez out for the rest of the regular season with a lower back strain (he is expected back during the postseason).
While Roberts would like to have a closer in the postseason, he acknowledged that it's more likely that he will play the matchups. At this time of year, some of the highest-leverage situations take place before the ninth inning, so having multiple options would free up Roberts to use his best relievers in the lanes that make sense.
"I think if there's an opportunity, for example, for Tanner to pitch a high-leverage inning in the seventh or the eighth inning, it's just hard to pass that up if he's the best option right there," Roberts said. "Because you just don't know where the ninth inning is going to be."

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are still fighting to keep their first-round bye, but they're already prepping for their 14th consecutive postseason appearance — and there are a number of questions they still need to answer.
Will Shohei Ohtani be ready? Does Edwin Díaz make the roster? Will Andy Pages be available? Is Roki Sasaki ready to return to his role as the Dodgers' vaunted postseason closer?
Every option to try to make up for these weaknesses is being considered. Even Hyeseong Kim, who has spent the majority of this season at Triple-A Oklahoma City.
"My expectation is Hyeseong will be here during the off-week and potentially be a conversation for the postseason — because he has the ability to run, play defense, and steal a base," Dave Roberts said, "So he's in the conversation, yes."
Alex Freeland is probably the most dispensable player on the Dodgers' active roster. If he's left behind, it'll be proof that their second base battle never truly declared a winner.
Dave Roberts hints at Hyeseong Kim return for Dodgers' postseason run
Kim was last seen in the majors from early April to late May. He was initially called up to replace Mookie Betts who went onto the injured list with an oblique strain. Kim hit .259 with a .651 OPS before being sent back down. His numbers in Triple-A have been nothing to write home about either (.675 OPS).
But Kim was on the Dodgers' postseason roster last season. His contributions were few — he earned a pinch-running appearance in the NLDS and was a defensive substitution during the World Series — and he didn't pick up a bat.
But Freeland is hot, and is hitting .375 with a 1.149 OPS over his last seven games. His ability to get on-base, the attribute that really put him on the map to begin with, has slowly come back to him. He has a .413 on-base percentage in September.
Clearly, this is a conversation the Dodgers are going to have to continue unless they trade one or both of these players. If Kim and Freeland survive the offseason together, they'll probably have to do it all over again next year.

item.title: [New York Post] Why Edwin Díaz still has hope of salvaging disaster debut Dodgers season
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: Ninth inning. Trumpets blaring. Edwin Díaz trotting out of the bullpen to collect the final three outs of a game. It’s a scene the Dodgers dreamt about all winter, after signing the star closer to a $69 million contract in December. It’s become an all-too-rare occurrence since then, with the right-hander battling injuries and underperformance in what has been a nightmarish debut season. item.content:encoded:
Ninth inning. Trumpets blaring. Edwin Díaz trotting out of the bullpen to collect the final three outs of a game.
It’s a scene the Dodgers dreamt about all winter, after signing the star closer to a $69 million contract in December.
It’s become an all-too-rare occurrence since then, with the right-hander battling injuries and underperformance in what has been a nightmarish debut season.
Yet, last Friday night, such a moment materialized again in Díaz’s return from the injured list — helping set the stage for a crucial final week in which the right-hander will battle for a place on the Dodgers’ postseason roster.
“I gotta show them I’m part of that bullpen,” Díaz said. “I haven’t pitched [much] this year, and when I’ve been on the mound, I’ve been struggling. So right now I’m giving my 200% just to show them I will be in that roster spot … Just every time, when they give me the ball in any situation, I will do my job.”
Granted, Friday’s outing wasn’t a save opportunity, with Díaz only pitching because the Dodgers held a comfortable six-run lead. Neither was his appearance in another rout of the Giants on Saturday, with the Dodgers continuing to ease him back in lower-leverage situations.
Still, at this point of the year, Díaz’s pair of scoreless innings were nonetheless signs of progress.
“I liked everything,” manager Dave Roberts said. “I liked his intensity. I liked the fastball velocity. The slider was good. So it was just really good to kind of get him back in the mix. That’s something to build on.”
Over this final week, the Dodgers will need to see more such outings. If Díaz is to make their postseason roster, he can no longer afford any bouts of regression.
“I just want to keep climbing the ladder,” Díaz said, “and finish the season strong.”
That Díaz is even in this spot is a reminder of all the ways his highly anticipated debut Dodgers season has gone wrong.
He stumbled through the opening month, suffering an ERA above 10.00, before being diagnosed with loose bodies in his elbow that required a surgical procedure.
When he returned in late July, his results still didn’t improve, with the 32-year-old giving up 11 more runs in nine more frustrating outings while continuing to battle flaws in his delivery.
Another injured list stint came in late August, when Díaz was shut down again with inflammation in his neck.
During that absence, he and the team tried to clean up his mechanics — specifically identifying a drop in his arm angle as a potential root cause of his problems this year. Yet, in his first four outings of a minor-league rehab assignment, he gave up six runs (including five in one disastrous appearance on Sept. 13) and walked seven batters.
As a result, just last week, Roberts openly cast doubt on Díaz’s postseason roster chances.

However, Díaz went back to the drawing board one more time during his stint in Triple-A. This time, he sat down with the club’s Oklahoma City pitching coaches, Ryan Dennick and David Anderson, to review old video from his three-time All-Star career.
That process yielded a new solution, with the trio finding that Díaz “wasn’t moving my hips the [same] way” he had in previous seasons.
Thus, Díaz made an adjustment in a bullpen session last week, looked good enough in one final rehab outing to be brought back to the majors and at least showed some signs of promise in his back-to-back outings last weekend — specifically by commanding his fastball better and allowing his slider to play off it deceptively.
“I’ve been able to throw strikes,” Díaz said, after striking out four batters and allowing just one hit and one walk in the two appearances. “I think that was my problem. I wasn’t throwing my fastball for strikes. Now I’m able to command my fastball really good. When I command my fastball, my slider plays up. So I feel really good right now.”
More improvement will be required, of course, if Díaz is to still salvage a spot on the team’s postseason roster.
He has already lost the closer role. He is battling with a slew of other right-handers, such as Blake Treinen and Brock Stewart, just for a middle relief gig.
It certainly isn’t what the Dodgers expected when they signed him in what felt like a coup back in December.
All they can hope for now is that, if the trumpets blare again in October, he has made enough progress to at least give them something out of the bullpen.
“It’s tough,” Díaz said. “But at the same time, I’m always positive. I know when I click, I click.”

item.title: [dodgersway.com] Dodgers map out Shohei Ohtani return with Roki Sasaki, Andy Pages roster moves

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are pacing toward having a first-round bye, avoiding the NL Wild Card round, and it would seem they are getting healthy at just the right time. The expectation in recent weeks was that Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages, and Roki Sasaki would return before the end of the regular season, and the Dodgers quietly revealed the roster moves to map everything out.
Updating their transaction log overnight, the Dodgers have reinstated Pages and Sasaki from the IL, and optioned Emmet Sheehan and Eliezer Alfonzo to the minors. With Ohtani eligible to be reinstated from the IL on Wednesday, the expectation is that Alex Freeland will be the corresponding move.
For Ohtani and Pages, the goal was simply having them back before the start of the playoffs. They now have a runway to shake off the rust over these next handful of games, before likely having next week off before playing in the NLDS.
Circumstances are a little more dire for Sasaki, who hasn't secured a spot on LA's playoff roster. Dave Roberts has already confirmed that Sasaki will be used out of the bullpen upon his return, and it goes to one of the biggest questions facing the Dodgers ahead of the playoffs.
The Dodgers are getting healthy just in time, but there are still answers needed
The Dodgers need to find answers in the bullpen. Ironically, the stage is set for Sasaki to repeat a similar shift he made last season. While the Dodgers have been adamant that Sasaki's future is as a starting pitcher, he was used as a quasi-finisher during the playoffs last year, and thrived.
Considering the questions surrounding Edwin Diaz and Edgardo Henriquez currently dealing with an injury, Sasaki once again becoming an effective high-leverage option for the Dodgers would be a major development for the playoffs.
The story of the Dodgers since the trade deadline has been that they are leaking oil. Sure, they traded for Tarik Skubal, but the operation looked faulty. With the returns of Sasaki, Pages, and Ohtani likely on Wednesday, they are finally reaching a level of healthy they haven't had for most of the season.
In other words, despite how uneven things have looked, the Dodgers are once again in a position to do whay they do best and flip the swith on during the month of October.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers notes: Is this team (and Edwin Diaz) playoff ready?
item.dc:creator: Andy Lane Chapman
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have managed to work their way out of their usual late summer lull, by going 14-5 so far in the month of September. But they face a test starting Tuesday to see if they really are in postseason form. This month, the Dodgers have beat up on below .500 teams in the Washington Nationals, Cincinnati Reds, and San Francisco Giants. But they have one last team with a winning record to face before the playoffs – the San Diego Padres. The Padres come in to this series winners of
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have managed to work their way out of their usual late summer lull, by going 14-5 so far in the month of September. But they face a test starting Tuesday to see if they really are in postseason form.
This month, the Dodgers have beat up on below .500 teams in the Washington Nationals, Cincinnati Reds, and San Francisco Giants. But they have one last team with a winning record to face before the playoffs – the San Diego Padres.
The Padres come in to this series winners of 13 of their last 14 games, needing two wins to secure a wildcard playoff spot. They have never made the playoffs three seasons in a row in the history of their franchise.
"I feel like the whole team is in a good spot right now," San Diego's Fernando Tatis Jr. told the San Diego Union-Tribune on Sunday. "We're playing really good baseball. We're checking in when we have to. The entire lineup is in a good spot right now. So when it's going like that, it's … a good time."
For their part, the Dodgers have a magic number of three to secure the second bye in the playoffs, which is important in setting the rotation that the Dodgers want.
"I think it's going to be a good kind of (playoff) primer," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of the upcoming series. "They're a very talented team. They're playing as good as anyone in all of baseball. I'm looking forward to playing those guys and just kind of ramping it up a little bit more for our guys."
Andy Pages is expected to be activated off the IL on Tuesday, hopefully fully healed and ready to add to the Dodgers offensive firepower.
Doug Padilla of the OC Register covers more of the details of what the Dodgers are thinking in their last six games of the season here.
One of the things still up in the air as far as the postseason roster goes is the status of Edwin Diaz, and if he can make a positive impact in the playoffs.
Diaz returned from the IL on Friday, a has two scoreless outings. But is that enough to get back on Dave Roberts' trust tree?
"It's been really disappointing," Díaz said of his season. "But now I've found growth to come back and perform the way everyone was expecting."
Diaz was on the IL earlier this season after having surgery on bone chips in his elbow and he came back ready to return to the leverage part of the bullpen. Except he wasn't actually ready.
Katie Woo of The Athletic covers all of the ins and outs of Diaz's return and playoff roster hopes here:
"Everybody was telling me I have a new elbow, so just keep going, keep climbing the ladder," Díaz said. "You will be fine. We trust you. They always stayed positive with me, and you know, I was positive too. I know when I'm right, I can do really good things. I just trusted the process with them. They stuck with me. They supported me. So I was OK."
But he wasn't ok. In his nine outings after returning from the IL, Diaz's ERA swelled to 11.85. He landed back on the IL with neck inflammation. So far in this return, he seems to be doing better. But with only six games left, he only has three to four games to prove he's playoff ready.
